title: AI-Native Family Office: What It Is and What It Means for a Household
description: What an AI-native family office is, why it exists now, and how it works for a household: one sourced record the family, its professionals, and their AI agents share.
h1: What is an AI-native family office?

blocks.text: Also called an AI family office
What is an AI-native family office?

An AI-native family office is a family office built for a world of abundant intelligence: one always-current, source-backed record of the household's entities, documents, and decisions that the family, its professionals, and their AI agents all work from, with the family approving what matters.

Your CPA, attorney, and advisor each hold part of the answer, and without a staffed office, connecting them tends to fall to the family. An AI-native family office gives that work one place to live. The family owns it, not any one advisor, firm, or AI model. It doesn't only work when a meeting is on the calendar: the documents, open questions, and answers are there whenever someone helping the family needs them, so the people and agents involved start from the same facts.
By Mat Silverstein, founder of X1 Wealth. Updated September 23, 2026.
Why this exists now
Some of this is measured, some is surveyed, and some is expert opinion or law. Each item says which.

items: A fixed level of AI capability got about 13x cheaper each year from 2023 to 2026 (Epoch AI).

Epoch AI measured the cost of a fixed level of AI performance falling about 47% a quarter, or 13x a year (September 2026). MIT FutureTech's independent estimate is 5x to 10x a year, and it finds the price of running the newest frontier models rising 3x to 18x a year (March 2026). What gets cheap is a given level of capability, not the newest model.
Epoch AI, September 22, 2026
· MIT FutureTech, March 23, 2026
People already using AI are using far more of it (Google and Menlo Ventures, 2026).

Google processes more than 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month across its products, up from about 480 trillion a year earlier (May 2026). Menlo Ventures estimates that global consumer spending on AI more than tripled in a year to $40 billion, while the share of US adults using AI rose only from 61% to 64% (September 2026). That suggests most of the new spending came from people already using it.
Google I/O, May 19, 2026
· Menlo Ventures, September 16, 2026
More partnership K-1s than in 2010, and fewer wealthy people using a single firm (IRS; Capgemini, 2026).

The IRS estimates that 30.2 million partnership Schedules K-1 were reported for tax year 2023, up from 22.4 million for tax year 2010. Those are forms, not households. Capgemini's 2026 World Wealth Report found that 19% of wealthy individuals worldwide worked with a single wealth firm in 2025, down from 39% in 2019.
IRS Publication 5035, tax year 2023 (Rev. 12-2025)
· IRS Publication 5035, tax year 2010
· Capgemini World Wealth Report, June 4, 2026
A staffed office still costs millions a year, and it still sends work out (J.P. Morgan and UBS, 2026).

Family offices in J.P. Morgan's 2026 survey spend $3 million a year on average to operate, and about $0.9 million even at $250 million or less in assets. Morgan Lewis, a law firm, puts the point where a single-family office generally begins to make sense at $100 million to $250 million in investable assets (July 2026). Even staffed offices send specialist work out: in UBS's 2026 survey, 75% outsource legal services and 59% outsource tax planning.
J.P. Morgan Private Bank, 2026 Global Family Office Report
· Morgan Lewis, July 14, 2026
· UBS Global Family Office Report 2026, p. 38
Agents are starting to act for people (Robinhood, a US appeals court, and the UK FCA, 2026).

Robinhood opened dedicated trading accounts for customers' AI agents in May 2026. In a case over an AI shopping assistant, a federal appeals court said in August 2026 that when a user directs the assistant, "it is the user who 'accesses'" Amazon's computers. That was an early-stage ruling under the federal computer fraud statute, not a rule about financial accounts. The review the UK Financial Conduct Authority commissioned from Sheldon Mills (July 2026) recommends that the FCA consider "structured and verifiable mandates (scope, limits and revocation)" for agents.
Robinhood, May 27, 2026
· Amazon.com Services v. Perplexity AI, 9th Cir., August 4, 2026
· FCA, The Mills Review, July 6, 2026

blocks.text: What is not measured yet

The trends above are measured or surveyed. The chain that would connect them for households is not, yet. It runs like this: cheaper intelligence produces more analysis, more analysis may make coordination between a family's professionals the constraint, and a record the household owns could help relieve it. That chain is our hypothesis. We have not found anyone who has measured it for households, and we say below what we are measuring. For counts of the entities and trusts behind household complexity, see our household entity statistics.
More AI answers can leave more to reconcile

A family, its CPA, and its attorney can each ask an assistant about the same K-1 now. If they start from different documents, someone still has to sort out which answer rests on the right facts. Without an office, that job tends to land on the family.

There is an old name for part of this. In 1865 William Stanley Jevons noticed that more efficient steam engines led Britain to burn more coal, not less. Something that looks like it is showing up in AI use: as analysis gets cheaper, people ask for more of it.

Inside one firm, AI can merge roles. Across a CPA, an estate attorney, and an advisor, it can't merge authority, because each is separately licensed and answers for their own work. Atlassian's 2026 survey of 12,035 knowledge workers put the general version plainly: "The real bottleneck isn't execution; it's coordination." Atlassian sells coordination software, so read that as a signal rather than proof.

We have not measured whether cheaper AI analysis creates more coordination work for households, and the research points both ways. Economists have found that some technologies decentralize work while others centralize it (Bloom, Garicano, Sadun, and Van Reenen, 2014), and the evidence that efficiency always raises total use is "far from conclusive" (Sorrell, 2009). Our view is narrower: when separately accountable professionals each produce more analysis, someone has to decide which version the family acts on.
Three ways the term is used today

The SEC's 2011 family office rule sets conditions for an exclusion from investment adviser regulation, including that a qualifying office does not hold itself out to the public as an investment adviser. X1 uses "family office" to describe the work it supports, not to claim that exclusion.
Institutional

Software and services that help an existing staffed office do more with fewer people: accounting, consolidated reporting, deal screening, and document extraction for a CFO and analysts. Much of what is written about the term today means this.
AI-enabled advisory firms
A wealth or advisory firm that offers a staffed service with AI underneath. The family hires the firm, and the firm keeps the record.
Household-owned
The family has the complexity of a family office but no staff. The office is a record the family owns, plus the professionals and agents who work from it. X1 is built around this meaning.
What an AI-native family office is made of

items.term: A record of what the family owns
items.def: Entities, trusts, properties, and accounts, and what belongs to what.
Facts drawn from documents keep a reference to the source document, and to the page when it is available, so anyone with access can check them.
When an assistant proposes a change to the record, a person the family has authorized reviews it before it is saved. Eligible changes can be undone afterward.
The CPA, attorney, and advisor work from what the family chooses to share with them, not from their own partial copies.
The family's own AI assistant works on the record through a connector, with the signed-in person's permissions.
Reading, drafting, a reversible change, and a commitment that can't be taken back each need a different level of approval.
It does not trade, move money, file taxes, draft legal documents, or replace a licensed professional's judgment.

blocks.text: Who checks, and who approves?
Say an assistant proposes filing a K-1 under one of the family's LLCs. Three separate questions need an answer:

items: What counts as true?
Which document, which version, confirmed by whom.
What can the system do?
Read, draft, change the record, or commit to something.
Who may approve it?
The family, or a professional the family has authorized for that kind of action.

blocks.text: Investors describe the shift in blunter terms. Sequoia Capital, in March 2026: "A copilot sells the tool. An autopilot sells the work." For the K-1, that means an assistant can propose where it belongs, and an authorized person checks the supporting document before the filing becomes part of the family's record. Institutional software settles these questions for an office's staff. A household-owned office settles them for the family.

One K-1, step by step in X1

X1 is an AI family office for complex households. The Alvarez family has an operating company, a rental LLC owned by their revocable trust, and a CPA, an estate attorney, and an advisor who have never been in the same meeting. In March, a K-1 arrives for the rental LLC.

items: The K-1 arrives in the family's X1 Vault, either uploaded or synced from a connected Box, Dropbox, or Google Drive folder.
An agent proposes filing it under the rental LLC and points to the part of the K-1 that supports the match.
The family confirms the filing. If the match was wrong, they undo it with one click.

The family shares a tax review with the CPA that includes the confirmed K-1, and the CPA opens it from an invitation. In the family's own record, the attorney's open question from last fall, whether the LLC was ever retitled to the trust, is still open next to the K-1.
Later, the family asks its own assistant in Claude what is still open for this year's return. The answer cites the record.

blocks.text: Nothing moved money, and nothing went to a professional until the family chose to share it. X1 doesn't watch every account or inbox on its own. Files from selected connected folders arrive in the Vault for review, and the record changes when an authorized person confirms a change. Connected folders are covered on the integrations page.
What to try first in X1

items: Start with one document
Add one document that matters, such as an operating agreement, a trust, or a K-1. See what X1 finds in it and confirm where it belongs.
Connect the folder you already keep
Connect a Box, Dropbox, or Google Drive folder you already use, so new files reach the record without being uploaded twice. Folder connections are part of X1 membership.
Share one question with one professional

Pick one open question and share a review with the professional who can answer it, then keep the answer with the decision it belongs to. If you don't have that professional yet, keep the question and its documents together in the record until you do. X1 doesn't supply their judgment.

blocks.text: Six questions to ask any AI family office

items: Who owns the record, and can you export all of it?
Can you see the source document behind every fact?
What can happen without your approval, and what can't?
Can your own CPA, attorney, and advisor work from it without switching firms?
Can your own AI assistant use it, and with whose permissions?
What happens to your data if you leave?

blocks.text: Who it is for

Your CPA has the tax documents, your attorney has the trust amendments, and you are the one who knows which version everyone should be using. Or you have the structure (a business, entities, trusts, properties) and are still working out which professionals you need.
X1 doesn't manage investments, and it doesn't replace the licensed professionals a family chooses.
Glossary

items.def: An AI-native family office is a family office built for a world of abundant intelligence: one always-current, source-backed record of the household's entities, documents, and decisions that the family, its professionals, and their AI agents all work from, with the family approving what matters.
The single place where a household's entities, documents, decisions, and open questions are kept, owned by the family rather than by any one advisor or firm.
A fact that links to the document and page it came from, so a family member or professional can check it.
The step where the person authorized for that action, usually a family member, approves a proposed change before it becomes part of the record.
The level of permission an action needs: reading, drafting, a reversible change, or a consequential commitment.
A question, document set, or review passed from the family to one professional, with the answer kept alongside the decision it belongs to.
A connection, built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), that lets an AI assistant such as Claude work on the household record under the signed-in person's permissions.

blocks.text: Coming soon
What we're measuring next

We're building a household finance workflow cost index. Token prices tell you what a word of AI output costs. They don't tell you what a finished, checkable piece of household work costs, because real work takes retries, tool calls, and review.

The index will use a fixed set of fictional household documents (operating agreements, trust documents, K-1s, an insurance policy) and fixed tasks, such as matching a K-1 to its entity or flagging a trust with no evidence it was funded. For each current model it will measure the full cost of a correctly completed, cited task, and it will be rerun every quarter. It uses no customer data.
Questions people ask
What is an AI-native family office?

An AI-native family office runs on one always-current record the family owns, where the household, its professionals, and their AI agents work from the same sourced facts, and nothing consequential happens without the family's approval.
Is an AI family office a wealth manager?

No. An AI family office keeps the household's record and coordinates the work around it. Investment management, trading, tax filing, and legal work stay with the licensed professionals the family chooses. X1 does not trade, move money, or give investment, tax, or legal advice.
Do I need a family office to use one?

No. The household-owned kind is built for families that already have the complexity of a family office, such as entities, trusts, properties, a business, and several professionals, without a staffed office to run it.
Does an AI family office move money?
X1 doesn't. It can prepare the facts and approvals around a decision, but trades and transfers happen at the family's custodian or bank, by the people authorized there.
How is it different from family office software?

Family office software usually serves an office's staff: accounting, consolidated investment reporting, or deal screening. A household-owned AI family office is the family's own record, which its professionals and agents work from. The family office software comparison covers the institutional tools job by job.
Can my CPA or attorney use it?

Yes, when the family shares work with them. In X1 a household can share a review, packet, or room with its CPA, attorney, or advisor. The professional signs in from the invitation and sees what was shared. They do not need to buy a practice plan.
Does it work in Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, or Muse?

Yes. X1 works in Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, and Meta's Muse. The assistant works with the permissions of the person who signed in, and when it proposes filing a document or adding an entity, X1 asks the person authorized for that action to confirm.
Is "AI-native" just a marketing term?
Often it is. The useful test is what a system can do without a person approving it, what it is not allowed to do, and who owns the record. The six questions on this page work for any provider.

blocks.text: In a world obsessed with 30-year retirement plans and passive index investing, we've entered a pivotal moment where the conventional wisdom is not just outdated—it's potentially dangerous. The convergence of intelligence technologies, unprecedented interest rates, and economic uncertainty has created what I call "The Great Wealth Reset." And those who recognize it will build fortunes while others struggle to keep pace.
The New Wealth Divide Is Real (And It's Not What You Think)

The wealth gap emerging in 2025 isn't simply between the rich and poor—it's between the high-agency and the low-agency. Between those who harness intelligence and those who remain dependent on outdated systems.

Consider this: The cost of intelligence is approaching zero. Information, analysis, and expertise that once required elite connections or expensive advisors is now available to anyone with the right tools. Yet most people remain chained to gatekeepers—financial advisors selling cookie-cutter plans, employers dictating their worth, institutions moving at a glacial pace.

The most revealing statistic? High-net-worth Millennials and Gen Z investors now allocate three times more of their portfolios to alternative investments than older generations. They're not playing by the old rules because they understand something fundamental: the playbook has changed.
Why Traditional Financial Advice Is Failing Today's Achievers

The uncomfortable truth: the financial establishment benefits when you follow conventional wisdom. The "save and wait" approach that worked in previous decades is woefully inadequate in today's environment where:

items: Interest rates hover at multi-decade highs
Credit card debt has reached a record $1.17 trillion
Intelligence technology is automating jobs while creating new wealth channels
39% of Americans now have side hustles to supplement their income

blocks.text: These aren't just economic shifts—they're seismic changes in how wealth is built and protected. Yet most financial advisors remain stuck in outdated paradigms, offering the same generic advice to wildly different individuals.
The 90-Day Implementation Gap
Here's what separates today's wealth builders from the rest: execution velocity.

While most people consume endless financial content without taking action, the new financial elite focus on implementation—fast, strategic moves that compound quickly. They understand what I call the "90-Day Rule":
The financial actions you take in the next 90 days will compound more dramatically than anything you'll do in the following 9 months.

Why? Because we're in an accelerated economic environment where early adopters of intelligence-enhanced strategies, tax optimizations, and alternative asset allocation are seeing outsized returns—while creating moats that become increasingly difficult for latecomers to overcome.
This isn't hyperbole; it's mathematics. Consider how quickly intelligence technology adoption doubled in just one year, or how forward-thinking professionals are already:

items: Analyzing potential investments in hours instead of weeks
Restructuring debt in the high-interest environment to free up cash flow
Implementing advanced tax strategies previously only available to the ultra-wealthy
Building multiple income streams with far less effort through automation

blocks.text: The Self-Reliance Imperative
Perhaps the most significant shift in today's wealth landscape is the rise of self-directed financial optimization.

The data is striking: 58% of wealthy Americans have already made financial adjustments due to rising rates, with younger wealthy investors being the most responsive (91%). They're not waiting for permission or guidance from traditional sources—they're taking control.

This self-reliance mindset is why we're seeing explosive growth in communities focused on implementation rather than just education. The modern wealth builder seeks structural knowledge and execution frameworks, not just theoretical concepts.
Breaking Free From Legacy Thinking

High agency is the currency of the Intelligence Economy. It means recognizing that you no longer need to entrust your financial future to people incapable of seeing or moving into the future. These anchors—whether they're outdated advisors, stagnant employers, or even friends and family with limiting mindsets—can dramatically restrict your wealth-building potential.

What once took months of research can now be accomplished in days. Strategies that required deep technical expertise are becoming accessible through purpose-built intelligence systems. This democratization of financial optimization is perhaps the most significant wealth-building opportunity of our lifetime.
The question is: Why would you continue to outsource your financial decision-making to those who benefit from your financial stagnation?
The Three-Step System the New Wealth Builders Are Using
After studying hundreds of successful cases and running countless simulations, I've identified a clear pattern among those who are thriving in this new environment:

1. Rapid Assessment - They use intelligence-powered tools to quickly identify their blind spots and hidden opportunities. When it comes to finance, that includes focusing on immediate cash flow improvements and tax efficiency. And it means honing in on strengths and quickly leveling up modern tooling to support those strengths.
2. Strategic Implementation - They execute high-impact moves in concentrated sprints, with the potential to unlock $10,000-$50,000 in value within 90 days.
3. Systematic Optimization - They create feedback loops that continuously refine their wealth-building systems as economic conditions and personal circumstances evolve.

This approach represents a fundamental shift from the "set it and forget it" mentality that dominated previous decades. It's active, adaptive, and aligned with how markets and technology actually work in 2025.
The 90-Day Execution Challenge
So here's my challenge to you: What if you dedicated the next 90 days to implementing rather than just learning? What if you focused on execution rather than endless consumption of financial content?

The results could be transformative. I've seen professionals free up $2,000+ in monthly cash flow, entrepreneurs identify tax strategies worth tens of thousands annually, and investors gain access to alternative investments they never knew existed—all within a 90-day implementation window.

It's a step-by-step execution framework with intelligence-powered tools that help you identify and implement strategies tailored to your specific situation.

It's never been a better time in our lifetimes to position accordingly, to build wealth. But doing so requires breaking free from the people and systems incapable of seeing—much less moving into—the future.

description: Compare Addepar alternatives by the job you need done: Orion, Black Diamond, Tamarac, Masttro, FundCount, Eton Solutions, and Aleta.
h1: 7 Addepar Alternatives for RIAs and Family Offices (2026)

blocks.text: 7 Addepar Alternatives for RIAs and Family Offices (2026)
Compare Addepar alternatives by the job you need done: Orion, Black Diamond, Tamarac, Masttro, FundCount, Eton Solutions, and Aleta.
By Mat Silverstein · Updated Aug 9, 2026

The best Addepar alternative depends on which part of Addepar you are trying to replace. Orion is the strongest alternative for an all-in-one RIA suite. Black Diamond is the closest fit for HNW reporting and client experience. Tamarac is strongest for RIA portfolio operations. Masttro is built around private family-office visibility. FundCount and Eton Solutions are stronger when accounting is central. Aleta is worth evaluating for a modern family-office data and reporting experience.
Last reviewed: August 9, 2026.
Start with the job, not the ranking
Most Addepar alternatives lists are written by a vendor that appears near the top. That does not make the products useless, but it makes the ranking predictable.

This guide does not name one universal winner. Addepar combines a data foundation, complex ownership modeling, reporting, analytics, and private-market workflows. A credible alternative must be compared against the part of that system your team actually needs.
A quick self-check
Name the job before you name a vendor.

items: Do you need better reports for clients?
Do you need deeper investment analysis?
Do you need trading and RIA operations?
Do you need books for trusts, funds, and family entities?
Do family members need a simpler view?
Is privacy the reason for the change?
Is price the problem, or is daily work the problem?

blocks.text: Write one sentence that begins, “We are replacing Addepar because…” If the team cannot finish it, the shortlist is premature.
A fast way to build the shortlist

items: Name the top job. Name who owns it.
Pick three hard cases. Remove all client names.
List each source of data. Mark who can grant access.
List the reports you must keep. Rank them by use.
Name the books of record. Do not blur books and reports.
Set a first-year budget. Add staff time to it.
Set a go-live date. Leave time for a test run.
Pick three firms. Give them the same cases.
Ask staff to score the work. Let sales staff watch.
Count each handoff. Count each manual fix.
Check each key fact. Trace it to its source.
Break one data feed. Watch how the team finds it.
Change one asset type. Check all linked reports.
Export the core data. Make sure the file can be used.
Price the full first year. Then price years two and three.
Call two client firms. Ask what went wrong at launch.
Write down each risk. Give each risk an owner.
Pick the best fit. Keep the score sheet on file.

head: Platform

blocks.text: X1 is not listed as an Addepar replacement because it is not one. X1 does not perform portfolio accounting, institutional analytics, custody, trading, or performance reporting.
1. Orion: best when the goal is RIA-suite consolidation

Orion is the most relevant alternative when a wealth firm wants to solve more than reporting. Its advisor technology suite covers CRM, planning, portfolio accounting, trading, compliance, risk, billing, reporting, and client experience.

Addepar is the more natural data and analytics core for complex investment environments. Orion is the more natural operating suite for an RIA that wants fewer vendors. Read the full Addepar vs Orion comparison.
Put Orion on the shortlist if: the firm wants one connected advisor ecosystem and Eclipse trading, Redtail, planning, and Denali AI are relevant to the target stack.
Prove in the demo: one end-to-end household workflow that crosses CRM, planning, trading, reporting, and compliance.
2. SS&C Black Diamond: best for HNW reporting and client experience

Black Diamond is a direct alternative when the buying team values polished portfolio reporting, household views, client portal experience, and support for complex wealth. SS&C has expanded the brand into a broader wealth solutions suite covering trading, CRM, compliance, trust, retirement, and investment services.

Addepar remains the stronger default for deep data flexibility, ownership modeling, and institutional analytics. Black Diamond can be the better fit when client reporting and the broader SS&C service environment matter more. See Addepar vs Black Diamond.
Prove in the demo: a complex family report with multiple entities, held-away assets, private investments, and different views for the principal and advisor.
3. Envestnet Tamarac: best for RIA portfolio operations
Tamarac is relevant when the core job is operating an RIA across trading, rebalancing, reporting, billing, CRM, client portal, proposals, and UMA workflows.
It is less of an Addepar look-alike than a different answer to the operating-model question. Addepar starts with data and analytics. Tamarac starts with the portfolio and practice workflow.
Prove in the demo: a restricted household rebalance carried through trading, reporting, billing, CRM follow-up, and the client portal.
4. Masttro: best for a private family-office operating view

Masttro positions itself around a family-office-native view of assets, entities, documents, alternatives, privacy, and multi-generational context. It is a credible alternative when family principals and office staff need one controlled estate-wide environment.

Addepar is stronger when institutional investment analytics and extensible data workflows drive the purchase. Masttro is stronger when private family-office visibility and principal access are the center of gravity. Read Masttro vs Addepar.
Prove in the demo: ownership and document workflows across trusts, LLCs, custodians, private assets, and family permissions.
5. FundCount: best when accounting must be native

FundCount is built around investment accounting, partnership accounting, general ledger, reporting, and family-office operations. It belongs on the shortlist when the office needs accounting authority, not only a reporting layer connected to separate books.

That can be a better architectural fit than Addepar for a family office whose hardest problem is closing books across entities and investments. It can also be a poor trade if the team mainly wants Addepar-style analytics and a polished advisor reporting experience.
Prove in the demo: one monthly close from source transaction through entity books, consolidation, allocation, reconciliation, and final report.
6. Eton Solutions AtlasFive: best for institutional family-office operations

Eton Solutions positions AtlasFive as a family-office platform spanning accounting, investments, documents, reporting, and workflows. It is relevant for offices that want a broad operating system with accounting at its center.

The diligence question is not whether AtlasFive has more categories than Addepar. It is whether the office wants to adopt Eton's operating model and has the scale, staff, and implementation discipline to use it.
Prove in the demo: a complete family-office workflow involving investment data, entity accounting, approvals, documents, and reporting.
7. Aleta: best for a modern family-office reporting shortlist

Aleta is a newer family-office platform focused on consolidated wealth data, reporting, and collaboration. It is worth considering when the buyer wants a modern experience and is willing to diligence a smaller vendor alongside established enterprise platforms.
Do not substitute a polished interface for proof. Verify custodian and private-asset coverage, data controls, reporting depth, service model, implementation capacity, and export rights.
Prove in the demo: the messiest real data set the office can safely provide, including missing fields, manual assets, permissions, and a correction workflow.

blocks.text: Score the result on completeness, explainability, manual work, review controls, client experience, and total implementation effort.
Where X1 fits

X1 sits around these systems rather than replacing them. The reporting or accounting platform can remain authoritative for investments and books. X1 keeps the broader household record connected: source documents, planning decisions, professional responsibilities, governance, and follow-through.
For a wider market view, see the family office software comparison and advisor platform comparison.

Frequently asked questions
Who competes with Addepar?

The relevant competitors depend on the use case. Orion, Black Diamond, and Tamarac compete for RIA platform decisions. Masttro, FundCount, Eton Solutions, and Aleta are relevant in family-office evaluations.
Is there a cheaper alternative to Addepar?
Possibly, but most enterprise vendors use custom quotes. A lower license price can still produce a higher total cost through implementation, integrations, accounting work, or manual reconciliation.
What is the best Addepar alternative for an RIA?

Orion is the strongest starting point for a broad all-in-one RIA suite. Black Diamond is compelling for HNW reporting, while Tamarac is compelling for portfolio operations. Test the finalists against the same workflows.
What is the best Addepar alternative for a family office?

Masttro is a strong privacy-first option. FundCount and Eton Solutions are more relevant when accounting is central. Black Diamond and Aleta may fit reporting-led offices. The right answer depends on the office's source-of-truth requirement.

title: Addepar vs Black Diamond in 2026: Verdict by Firm Type
description: They get shortlisted together and lose to each other for different reasons. Compared on alternatives, reporting, AI, and what each really costs to implement.
h1: Addepar vs Black Diamond in 2026: Verdict by Firm Type

blocks.text: Addepar vs Black Diamond in 2026: Verdict by Firm Type
They get shortlisted together and lose to each other for different reasons. Compared on alternatives, reporting, AI, and what each really costs to implement.
By Mat Silverstein · Updated Aug 10, 2026

Addepar and Black Diamond both serve the high-net-worth and family office market, but they come from different directions. Addepar was built for institutional-grade portfolio analytics and complex alternative investments. Black Diamond evolved from advisor-focused reporting into a unified wealth platform under the SS&C umbrella. As of March 2026, Addepar manages roughly $9 trillion across 1,400+ firms, while Black Diamond serves 3,000+ firms with $3.6 trillion in assets under administration.

This guide helps wealth managers and family offices evaluate which platform fits their complexity level, covers the major 2026 product updates (including Addepar's Addison AI and Black Diamond's new Investment Management Services), and identifies what client-facing planning tools neither provides.
Last reviewed: March 14, 2026.
Key takeaways

items: Addepar is often chosen when institutional-grade analytics and complex reporting are the priority.
Black Diamond is often chosen when client presentation and advisor workflow usability matter most.
The biggest risk is implementation: data conversion, valuation workflows, and reporting standards.
Neither platform keeps the decisions behind the numbers or coordinates the professionals around the household. Both report what you own; neither holds what you decided, why, or who is handling it.

blocks.text: Quick verdict

Choose Addepar if: You have significant alternative investments and need institutional-grade analytics. Addepar is often evaluated for sophisticated portfolio attribution and complex reporting, but it tends to require deeper implementation and dedicated operational ownership.

Choose Black Diamond if: You're a wealth advisor or smaller family office that needs excellent reporting without Addepar's complexity. Black Diamond is often evaluated for strong reporting and alternative-asset servicing through SS&C’s ecosystem, with a more accessible interface and typically a lighter implementation footprint.

Consider X1 Wealth as a complement if: You want one record your clients and their other professionals all work from (the decisions, the source-backed holdings by entity, the documents) on top of what your reporting platform already shows. Neither Addepar nor Black Diamond keeps the decisions behind the numbers or coordinates across the professionals around the household.
Comparison at a glance
Implementation checklist (what to do before you sign)

items: Inventory data sources (custodians, alts administrators, private holdings).
Define householding and entity rollups (trusts, LLCs, foundations).
Lock reporting standards (performance methodology, benchmarks, valuations).
Plan a parallel reporting period before switching client views.
Assign an owner for data hygiene and ongoing reconciliation.
Validate alternative asset workflows (capital calls, distributions, valuations).

blocks.text: Understanding Addepar

Addepar is commonly evaluated for complex wealth reporting. Founded in 2009, it is used by over 1,400 firms across nearly 60 countries that need sophisticated reporting and analytics for multi-entity and alternative-heavy portfolios.
What sets Addepar apart
1. Alternative investment depth
Addepar was built for alternatives. The platform handles:

items: Private equity fund structures and capital calls
Hedge fund performance attribution
Real estate portfolio tracking
Venture capital investments
Art, collectibles, and other illiquid assets
Complex partnership structures and waterfall calculations

blocks.text: Some teams also evaluate Addepar’s alternative-asset workflows for reducing manual data entry during document-heavy operations (capital calls, distributions, statements). Validate the exact ingestion and review workflow in your demo. If you are the investor receiving those notices rather than the team processing them, our capital call notice checklist lists the fields to check before any money moves.
2. Institutional-grade analytics
Addepar's analysis tools go beyond basic performance reporting:

items: Sophisticated attribution analysis
Risk decomposition across complex portfolios
Custom analytics and factor modeling
Scenario analysis and stress testing

blocks.text: For firms managing institutional capital or serving the most sophisticated clients, these capabilities matter.
3. Workflow and automation

Both platforms offer workflow support to reduce manual data entry and improve servicing. The key diligence question is whether those workflows map cleanly to your actual data sources, alternative investment processes, and reporting standards.
4. Addison AI (launched March 2026)

Addepar's native AI assistant lets investment professionals query portfolio data in natural language. Ask about performance drivers, exposure concentrations, or liquidity positions and get answers grounded in actual portfolio context with traceable sources.

Addison builds on earlier AI capabilities: Alts Data Management (machine learning plus human verification to extract private markets data) and Intelligent Statements (transforms unstructured financial statements into review-ready files). Addepar acquired Arcus, an AI workflow startup, in May 2025 to accelerate this work.

The roadmap includes proactive insight delivery with market-aware context and agentic workflows for data remediation, client intelligence, and reporting. If your evaluation hinges on AI-assisted portfolio analysis, ask Addepar for a live Addison demo with your actual data.
Addepar pricing
Addepar uses custom, quote-driven pricing. They don't publish rates, but expect:

items: Premium pricing reflecting institutional positioning
Custom quotes based on size, modules, and firm complexity
Significant implementation costs for complex deployments

blocks.text: Addepar is primarily for large-scale firms. Smaller RIAs may find it over-engineered and cost-prohibitive.
Addepar limitations

items: Steep learning curve.
Requires dedicated power users who understand both the platform and alternative investment operations
Long implementation.
Months for complex deployments (scope-dependent)
Technical resources required.
Not a "set it and forget it" platform
Overkill for simpler portfolios.
If you don't have significant alternatives, Addepar's complexity may not be justified

blocks.text: Understanding Black Diamond

In August 2025, SS&C consolidated its wealth management products under a single brand: SS&C Black Diamond Wealth Solutions. The unified platform now spans portfolio management, CRM, compliance, trading, trust services, and investment management. It serves over 3,000 firms managing $3.6 trillion in assets, with 800,000+ active users and 70 of the top 100 Barron's-ranked RIAs on the platform.
Black Diamond bridges the gap between advisor-focused reporting and family office capabilities. It's more accessible than Addepar while still handling complex wealth situations.
What sets Black Diamond apart
1. Advisor-friendly complexity
Black Diamond makes complex reporting accessible without requiring an army of analysts. The platform handles:

items: Multi-custodian aggregation
Alternative asset servicing
Multi-entity structures (trusts, LLCs, foundations)
Consolidated household reporting

blocks.text: The interface is more intuitive than Addepar's for users who aren't full-time platform specialists.
2. Operational alt servicing
While Addepar excels at alternative asset reporting, Black Diamond excels at alternative asset servicing:

items: Automated data collection and processing
Capital call and distribution tracking
Document management and audit trails
Integration with SS&C's vast alternative investment ecosystem

blocks.text: 3. Client portal
Black Diamond’s client portal is commonly evaluated for:

items: Configurable dashboards with performance and projections
Two-way secure document vault
Outside account aggregation
Detailed balance sheet reporting
Mobile accessibility

blocks.text: 4. SS&C ecosystem advantages
As part of SS&C Technologies, Black Diamond benefits from:

items: Deep custodial integrations
Alternative investment data feeds
Compliance and regulatory tools
Third-party integration ecosystem (scope varies by deployment)

blocks.text: 5. Investment Management Services (launched July 2025)
Black Diamond added a full investment management suite in mid-2025:

items: Managed Account Services
: outsource trading, rebalancing, and portfolio oversight directly from the platform, powered by SS&C ALPS Advisors
Model Marketplace
: curated access to portfolio models from SS&C ALPS and third-party managers
Proposal Generation
: automated tools for building investment proposals and accelerating client onboarding
Household-Level Rebalancing
: tax-aware optimization aligned to individual client goals and constraints

blocks.text: 6. eMoney planning integration (November 2025)

Black Diamond integrated with eMoney Advisor for embedded financial planning. Advisors can deliver data-driven planning without switching platforms. This closes a gap that previously required separate planning software.
Black Diamond also won the 2026 WealthTech Americas Award for Best CRM Provider, reflecting the platform's expansion beyond pure reporting.
Black Diamond pricing
Black Diamond pricing is quote-driven and often structured around firm scale and services. Treat any “rule of thumb” pricing you hear as budgeting guidance, not a quote.
Black Diamond limitations

items: Less analytical depth.
Good reporting, but not Addepar-level analytics for institutional portfolios
No native AI assistant.
Addepar's Addison is ahead here. Black Diamond has not announced a comparable natural-language query tool
May outgrow.
Very complex family offices with heavy alternative portfolios may eventually need Addepar's attribution and factor modeling

blocks.text: Feature-by-feature breakdown
Alternative investment handling
Addepar: Strong alternative asset support and analytics. Sophisticated valuation workflows, performance attribution, partnership accounting, and document/data ingestion support.
Black Diamond: Strong operational servicing through SS&C's alternative investment ecosystem. Excellent at data collection, processing, and integration. Better for servicing than deep analytics.
Winner: Addepar for complex alternative portfolios and analytics. Black Diamond for operational efficiency in alternative servicing.
Portfolio analytics
Addepar: Institutional-grade analytics including risk decomposition, factor modeling, attribution analysis, and scenario testing. Built for investment committees and sophisticated clients.
Black Diamond: Solid performance reporting and visualization. Functional analytics but not designed for institutional-level analysis.
Winner: Addepar, clearly.
Data aggregation
Addepar: Broad connectivity with sophisticated data reconciliation and normalization. Handles complex multi-source data well.
Black Diamond: Strong connectivity through SS&C's ecosystem and custodial partnerships. Reliable aggregation with good data quality.
Winner: Tie. Both handle multi-custodian aggregation well.
Client portal
Addepar: Comprehensive client portal with customizable views and reporting. Functional but designed more for sophisticated users.
Black Diamond: Intuitive client portal with configurable dashboards, a document vault, and balance sheet reporting. Often more accessible for typical HNW clients.
Winner: Black Diamond for client experience and accessibility.
Implementation and support
Addepar: Implementation is typically months and scope-dependent. Often requires dedicated technical resources and power users, plus ongoing maintenance.
Black Diamond: Implementation is typically months and scope-dependent, with an accessible learning curve and often less ongoing technical burden.
Winner: Black Diamond for faster, smoother implementation.
Trading and investment management
Addepar: Offers trading and rebalancing capabilities depending on modules and configuration. Confirm whether your use case requires separate systems.

Black Diamond: Added Investment Management Services in mid-2025, including managed account services through SS&C ALPS, a model marketplace, and household-level tax-aware rebalancing. This narrows the gap with dedicated TAMP platforms.
Winner: Black Diamond has moved ahead here with the IMS suite, especially for firms that want managed account capabilities built into their reporting platform.
Pricing accessibility
Addepar: Premium institutional pricing. Cost-prohibitive for many mid-sized firms.
Black Diamond: Often more accessible than Addepar for firms that don't need full institutional analytical depth.
Winner: Black Diamond for cost-effectiveness.
Who should choose Addepar?
Addepar is right for you if:

items: You support complex alternative investments and multi-entity reporting
You need institutional-grade analytics and attribution
You have technical resources for implementation and ongoing maintenance
Your clients expect sophisticated investment committee-level reporting
Complex partnership structures and illiquid assets are common
You're willing to invest in a multi-month implementation

blocks.text: Ideal Addepar firm: A multi-family office or large RIA with dedicated operations and a need for institutional-quality analytics across complex holdings.
Who should choose Black Diamond?
Black Diamond is right for you if:

items: You serve HNW clients with complex (but not ultra-institutional) needs
Alternative assets are important but not the dominant portfolio component
You want strong reporting without requiring dedicated platform specialists
Implementation speed and operational simplicity matter for your timeline
Client portal experience is a competitive differentiator
You prefer SS&C's ecosystem and custodial integrations

blocks.text: Ideal Black Diamond firm: A wealth manager or single-family office serving clients with alternatives exposure, wanting premium reporting and client experience without Addepar's complexity and cost.
What if you're not UHNW?

Both Addepar and Black Diamond were designed for institutional-scale firms and ultra-high-net-worth clients. If you're a wealth advisor serving clients with $500K to $5M in assets, or a household with multiple entities and advisors but not $25M in investable assets, the standard playbook doesn't quite fit.

The honest assessment: Addepar's pricing and implementation overhead is hard to justify below roughly $1B in firm AUM. Black Diamond is more accessible, but the full platform still assumes dedicated operations staff and complex custodial relationships.

For advisors serving the mass-affluent and lower-HNW segment, consider what your clients actually need beyond reporting. Often it's coordination between their CPA, estate attorney, and insurance professional. It's governance documents they can share with a spouse. It's a clear explanation of their trust structure. These are family-office-grade deliverables that neither reporting platform provides, regardless of your AUM tier.

If you're evaluating platforms for this segment, see our virtual family office guide for what a technology-enabled VFO looks like at a fraction of the traditional cost, or our family office software comparison for the full market landscape including options under $1,000/month.
What neither platform offers

Both Addepar and Black Diamond produce excellent investment reporting. They show clients what they own, how it's performing, and how it's allocated. But neither addresses what wealthy families increasingly ask for:
Values and governance frameworks
Neither platform helps families articulate:

items: What do they actually care about beyond returns?
How do they make financial decisions together?
What's the governance structure for family wealth?

blocks.text: You're building these deliverables manually or not at all.
Legacy and estate planning context
Your reporting shows a large balance sheet. Great. But:

items: Does the family understand their estate documents?
Are beneficiaries aligned with the actual plan?
Is the next generation prepared?

blocks.text: Neither platform addresses the human side of wealth transfer.
Client-ready strategic documents
Both produce excellent reports. But what documents help family members understand the strategy, not just the numbers?
X1 Wealth: for what reporting platforms miss

X1 does not compete with Addepar or Black Diamond for portfolio reporting. Both are excellent at it. X1 is the coordination layer above the reporting, where a complex household and the professionals who advise it work from one record.

One shared household record: the decisions behind the numbers (what was decided, why, who owns the next step), a source-backed register of what the household owns by entity, plus the documents and Pulse telemetry, all in one place the household and its CPA, attorney, and advisor work from. Import an Addepar or Black Diamond export, or read the statements the family uploads, and it lands in the register with the source on file.

Decision Memory: a running record of what the family decided and why, with follow-up checkpoints to revisit it. The reasoning a reporting platform never keeps. And it compounds: the longer a family uses X1, the more of their decision history lives in one place, the part a reporting platform cannot reconstruct after the fact.
Advisor Packets and coordination: source-linked bundles that prep the family and their other professionals for a meeting, so nothing slips between the people who each see only their slice.
The why, documented: Family Constitution, the Family Office Blueprint, and plain-English estate-plan summaries turn the numbers into context the family can actually read.
Best for: Family offices using Addepar or Black Diamond who want the decision-and-coordination layer those reporting platforms leave out, without building it from scratch.

h1: Addepar vs Orion (2026): Which Wealth Platform Fits Your RIA?

blocks.text: Addepar vs Orion (2026): Which Wealth Platform Fits Your RIA?
Addepar is built around complex investment data and analytics. Orion is a broader RIA operating suite. Compare fit, AI, implementation, pricing, and demo questions.
By Mat Silverstein · Updated Aug 9, 2026

Addepar is the stronger fit for firms that need institutional-grade data, complex ownership reporting, and private-market analytics. Orion is the stronger fit for RIAs that want CRM, planning, portfolio accounting, trading, compliance, and reporting from one connected vendor. Neither is simply “better.” They are built around different operating models.
Last reviewed: August 9, 2026.
The short answer
Choose Addepar when your hard problem is making complicated wealth data usable: alternatives, multiple entities, currencies, ownership structures, custom reporting, and investment analysis.

Choose Orion when your hard problem is running an advisory firm across many connected workflows with fewer vendors. Orion brings CRM, planning, portfolio accounting, trading, compliance, risk, and reporting into a broad suite.

Keep both on the shortlist if you are a large RIA, multifamily office, or private wealth team. The decision usually turns on whether the firm wants an analytics-first data core or an all-in-one operating suite.
Addepar vs Orion at a glance

head: Decision

blocks.text: Public feature pages do not provide enough information to calculate a reliable total cost for either platform. Treat any third-party price estimate as a lead for the sales conversation, not as a budget.
A quick self-check
Ask these questions before you book a demo.

items: Do private funds and complex entities consume much of your team's time?
Do you have staff who can own data rules and custom reports?
Is trading part of this purchase, or is it already solved?
Are you trying to remove other tools from the stack?
Will clients use the system, or will staff prepare the output for them?
Which current handoff creates the most errors?

blocks.text: If complex data is the main pain, begin with Addepar. If disconnected firm workflows are the main pain, begin with Orion. If both are true, keep both and insist on the same demo case.

Set the rules before either sales call. Name one lead. Pick three hard client cases. Remove all client names. List the work that must stay in house. List the work a vendor may own. Set a first-year budget. Set a go-live date. Agree on how the team will score each test. Keep the same rules for both firms. Do not change the test after a good demo.
The decision most comparisons miss
A feature checklist makes these platforms look more alike than they are. A better question is: what do you want the platform to organize?

items: Addepar organizes complex investment data so a team can analyze it, report on it, and see through legal ownership structures.
Orion organizes the work of an advisory firm across client, portfolio, trading, planning, compliance, and reporting systems.

blocks.text: That distinction affects staffing, integrations, implementation, and exit risk. An Addepar-centered firm often builds specialized workflows around a powerful data and reporting core. An Orion-centered firm often accepts more of one vendor's operating model in exchange for fewer handoffs between systems.
Where Addepar is stronger
Complex ownership and alternatives

Addepar's public platform materials emphasize a unified data foundation, flexible reporting, private-market data, ownership modeling, and analytics across asset classes. Its alternatives materials describe workflows for fund statements, capital calls, distributions, benchmarking, and liquidity analysis.

That makes Addepar a natural finalist when the portfolio includes private equity, venture funds, real estate, partnerships, trusts, and layered entities. The value is not merely seeing an outside asset on a dashboard. It is preserving the structure and context needed for serious analysis.
Custom reporting and data access

Addepar is also the stronger starting point when an investment or reporting team wants a flexible data layer that can support tailored views, APIs, and downstream workflows. Firms with dedicated operations or data staff can make more use of that flexibility than a small practice with no platform owner.
Scale signals

Addepar says its platform serves more than 1,400 client firms in over 60 countries and represents more than $9 trillion in assets. Those are vendor-reported scale figures, not a measure of fit. They do show that Addepar is built for large, complex data environments.
Where Orion is stronger
One connected RIA suite

Orion's advisor technology platform spans CRM, financial planning, portfolio accounting, trading, compliance, risk, billing, reporting, and client experience. Orion says its open platform connects with more than 100 partners and that 17 of the top 20 firms on Barron's 2026 Top RIA Firms list use Orion technology.
This breadth matters when the firm's main problem is operational fragmentation. Instead of choosing separate systems for every job, an RIA can standardize more of the workflow inside Orion.
Trading and advisor operations

For firms where model management, rebalancing, account workflows, billing, and day-to-day advisor operations drive the purchase, Orion starts closer to the full operating requirement. Addepar can be part of that environment, but it is not positioned as the same kind of end-to-end RIA suite.
Denali AI

Orion's Denali AI materials describe three layers: AI embedded in Orion products, packaged Denali solutions, and an enterprise offering. Orion says Denali can work across CRM, planning, portfolio, and risk data in a firm-isolated environment, with financial-professional review built into the process.
The useful demo question is not “does it have AI?” Ask which exact data sources the assistant can use, which actions it can take, how a person reviews the result, and what is recorded for compliance.
A practical RFP scorecard
Do not let both vendors give polished demos against different scenarios. Send the same five cases in advance and score the completed output.

head: Test case
Evidence to request
rows: One family with trusts, LLCs, private funds, and multiple custodians
A capital call, distribution, and revised valuation carried through reporting
A model change, restrictions, cash need, and household-level review
A complete meeting package built from current data
One wrong classification corrected, approved, and reflected everywhere

blocks.text: Score each case on time, manual steps, data lineage, reviewer controls, and the quality of the client-facing result. A long feature list cannot answer those questions.
Migration questions to settle before signing

items: Who owns householding, entity, and security classifications after launch?
Which historical data will be converted, and which will remain in an archive?
How will private assets and missing data be identified during the parallel run?
Which integrations are supported by the vendor, and which become your problem?
Can the firm export normalized data, documents, and configuration if it leaves?
What does the total first-year cost include: implementation, data conversion, training, connectors, and additional modules?

blocks.text: Run the old and new systems in parallel long enough to reconcile several representative households. The goal is not identical screenshots. It is confidence that balances, performance, ownership, fees, and client reports remain explainable.
Where X1 fits

X1 does not replace Addepar or Orion. Those platforms run investment data and advisory operations. X1 adds a shared planning and coordination record around the household: documents, decisions, open questions, professional handoffs, and follow-through across the advisor, CPA, attorney, and family.
For more context, compare Addepar with Black Diamond, see Orion vs Black Diamond, or use the broader advisor platform guide.
Browse every X1 comparison or see how X1 works with an advisor's existing stack.
Frequently asked questions
Is Addepar a competitor to Orion?

Yes, particularly for large RIAs and wealth firms evaluating a portfolio data and reporting core. The overlap is real, but Addepar is more analytics-first while Orion offers a broader connected operating suite.
Which is better for a family office?

Addepar is usually the more natural fit when complex ownership, private assets, and investment reporting drive the purchase. A multifamily office that also wants a broad advisor operating suite should evaluate Orion against the same real client cases.
Does either company publish pricing?

Neither publishes a standard price that is sufficient for a reliable comparison. Request an itemized three-year quote that includes conversion, implementation, integrations, support, and the exact modules in scope.
Can X1 replace Addepar or Orion?
No. X1 is not portfolio accounting, trading, custody, or performance reporting software. It complements those systems by organizing household planning context and coordination.

If sophisticated reporting is the priority, add Black Diamond and Addepar to the shortlist. Wealthbox handles CRM, Nitrogen handles risk and proposals, and X1 carries household context across the client's financial team.

The hard part is knowing what each platform actually owns. A vendor may receive data from several custodians without routing trades to all of them. A polished reporting system may still need a separate rebalancer. This guide separates those jobs, compares eight platforms, and gives you the questions to use in a live demo.

blocks.text: Platform deep dives
1. Orion (+ Denali AI)
Best for: RIAs wanting to consolidate CRM, trading, reporting, planning, and compliance under one vendor.
Ideal firm size: $200M to $10B+ AUM. The Foundation Stack offers entry-level pricing for smaller firms.
What Orion does well:

Orion has grown from a portfolio accounting tool into the most comprehensive all-in-one wealth platform. The ecosystem now includes Redtail CRM, Orion Planning, Eclipse trading and rebalancing, HiddenLevers risk analytics, and Brinker Capital investment management. As of December 2025, the platform manages approximately $5.8 trillion in assets across 8 million accounts. 17 of the top 20 Barron's RIA firms use Orion technology.

Eclipse remains the industry standard for trading and rebalancing. Household-level trading, tax-loss harvesting, and model management give advisors institutional-grade execution. This is Orion's deepest competitive advantage.
2026 update: Denali AI Enterprise
Orion launched Denali AI Enterprise in February 2026. The system pulls data from CRM, planning, portfolio management, and risk tools into a single connected view. Two AI assistants are live:

items: Report Assistant
creates client-ready report drafts using firm templates, cutting formatting and assembly time.
Query Studio
lets operations teams ask questions in plain English and pull complex data without SQL or internal requests.

blocks.text: Orion has announced plans for additional AI assistants covering proposal generation, account opening, billing, and reconciliation. Denali AI is available as a flat monthly subscription (pricing adjusts based on usage patterns).
Pricing:

Quote-driven and modular. The Foundation Stack bundles portal, planning, portfolio accounting, billing, and reporting at an entry-level price point. Custom Indexing runs at a published 0.15% fee. Full platform quotes depend on AUM, modules, and firm complexity.
Limitations:

items: The breadth creates a steep learning curve and usually calls for dedicated operations staff.
Some interface components feel older than point solutions built in the last five years.
Deep integration makes switching platforms costly. Evaluate the exit path before you sign.

2. Black Diamond (SS&C)
Best for: Wealth managers and family offices serving HNW/UHNW clients where reporting quality and alternative asset handling are competitive differentiators.
Ideal firm size: $500M to $10B+ AUM. 70 of the top 100 Barron's-ranked RIAs use the platform.
What Black Diamond does well:

In August 2025, SS&C consolidated its wealth management products under a single brand: SS&C Black Diamond Wealth Solutions. The unified platform now spans portfolio management, CRM, compliance, trading, trust services, and investment management. It serves over 3,000 firms managing $3.6 trillion in assets with 800,000+ active users.

Black Diamond's client portal is consistently rated among the best in the industry: configurable dashboards, a two-way document vault, outside account aggregation, and detailed balance sheet reporting. For firms where client presentation quality wins business, this matters.

items: Investment Management Services (July 2025):

Best for: Enterprise RIAs that use unified managed accounts (UMA) and want portfolio management, trading, reporting, and CRM in an integrated Envestnet ecosystem.
Ideal firm size: $500M to $10B+ AUM. Mid-to-large RIAs managing complex model portfolios.

Tamarac is Envestnet's integrated platform for independent advisors, combining portfolio management, rebalancing, reporting, billing, client portal, CRM, data aggregation, and unified managed accounts. It holds approximately 11% market share in the performance reporting category (Kitces 2023 tech survey), placing it second behind Orion's 20%.

The platform's strength is in model management and trading infrastructure. For firms running UMA programs or managing multiple model strategies across a large client base, Tamarac provides the scale that smaller platforms cannot.

Evolution of Report Builder with pie chart visuals, expanded attribution columns, and security-level details.

blocks.text: Pricing:
Quote-driven. Tamarac asks firms to request pricing. Expect enterprise-tier costs structured around firm size and selected modules.
Limitations:

items: Envestnet ecosystem lock-in. Moving away from Tamarac means leaving the broader Envestnet data and investment infrastructure.
Steeper learning curve than Advyzon or Wealthbox.
No native AI assistant announced for 2026 (though Envestnet has broader AI initiatives across the parent company).

blocks.text: 4. Addepar
Best for: RIAs and multi-family offices that need institutional-grade analytics, complex alternative investment modeling, and sophisticated portfolio attribution.
Ideal firm size: $1B+ AUM. Firms with dedicated operations teams and significant alternative allocations.
What Addepar does well:

Addepar reports more than $9 trillion in assets across 1,400+ firms in nearly 60 countries. The platform's Financial Graph models complex ownership structures, fund hierarchies, and partnership waterfalls. That depth serves firms with active investment committees or CIOs working across attribution, risk decomposition, and factor modeling.
2026 update: Addison AI

Addepar launched Addison, its native AI assistant, in March 2026. Addison lets investment professionals query portfolio data in natural language, asking about performance drivers, exposure concentrations, or liquidity positions and receiving answers grounded in actual portfolio context with traceable sources.

Addison builds on earlier AI capabilities: Alts Data Management (machine learning plus human verification for private markets data extraction) and Intelligent Statements (transforms unstructured financial statements into review-ready files). The roadmap includes proactive insight delivery and agentic workflows for data remediation and client intelligence.
Pricing:

Custom, quote-driven. No published rates. Premium pricing reflecting institutional positioning. Industry estimates range from $75K to $250K+ annually for comprehensive implementations. Costs scale with AUM.
Limitations:

items: Requires dedicated technical resources and power users. Many family principals never log in directly.
Implementation takes months for complex deployments.
Overkill and cost-prohibitive for firms without significant alternative investments.

blocks.text: Existing comparisons: Addepar vs Black Diamond | Masttro vs Addepar
5. Nitrogen (formerly Riskalyze)

Nitrogen focuses on risk, proposals, and the client conversation. Its Risk Number gives the advisor and client a shared way to discuss risk tolerance before implementation moves into the portfolio system.

The Risk Number, built on Nobel Prize-winning academic frameworks, gives prospects and clients a concrete score. Nitrogen reports use by more than 50,000 advisors. The score gives an investment conversation a measurable starting point.
Firm size: Solo advisors to large RIAs. Pricing scales per-advisor or by account count.

2024 expansion: In July 2024, Nitrogen launched three products simultaneously: Risk Center (core risk alignment), Planning Center (financial planning), and Research Center (investment research). This moves the platform from a single-purpose tool toward a broader client engagement suite, though the newer products are still maturing against established alternatives like eMoney and RightCapital.
Pricing: Starts at $99/month for the Riskalyze plan. Higher tiers (Nitrogen Growth, Nitrogen Complete) add planning, research, and premium support. Team solutions use accounts-based pricing.

Where Nitrogen fits in a stack: It sits alongside a portfolio core such as Orion, Black Diamond, Tamarac, or Advyzon as the proposal and engagement layer. The rebrand from Riskalyze changed the name while keeping the underlying product familiar to existing users.
6. Advyzon

Nine consecutive years as the #1 rated all-in-one platform in the T3/Inside Information Software Survey. That tells you something about what advisors actually want: portfolio management, reporting, trading, CRM, billing, and document storage integrated without the steep learning curve of enterprise platforms.
Firm size sweet spot: $50M to $2B AUM. Advyzon is designed for firms managing several hundred client accounts with a lean operations team.

The Quantum rebalancer handles tax harvesting, location optimization, and cash management. Customizable dashboards let your portfolio manager, office manager, and advisor each see different data from the same system. The platform connects with Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace natively, so emails and appointments show up in client records without manual logging.

For firms growing into the HNW space, Advyzon offers Auria for family offices and UHNW clients, plus Advyzon Investment Management (AIM) for firms that want investment solutions alongside the technology.

Pricing: From $6,500/year for up to 150 client accounts, scaling in tiers. This is one of the few platforms with transparent pricing. Compare that to the "request a quote" experience with Orion, Black Diamond, or Tamarac.

Where Advyzon runs into limits: Enterprise-scale firms ($5B+ AUM) may outgrow it. Eclipse (Orion) still leads for institutional-scale trading. Some enterprise features are still catching up to the larger platforms, though the pace of development is fast.
7. Wealthbox

Wealthbox exists because advisors kept choosing Salesforce and then regretting the complexity, or choosing Redtail and then wanting something more modern. It is the second most-used CRM among advisors (T3 survey), designed for financial advisors from the ground up.

The interface is clean. Adoption is fast. Integration coverage is broad: 150+ custodial and wealthtech connections. Contact management, activity streams, task management, and visual relationship mapping through Asset-Map integration handle the relationship tracking without Salesforce's configuration overhead.

2026 addition: An AI note-taker that records, transcribes, and generates actionable notes from client meetings. For solo advisors and small teams, this eliminates one of the biggest post-meeting time sinks.
Where Wealthbox fits: It is the relationship layer in a multi-vendor stack. Pair it with Orion, Black Diamond, or Advyzon for portfolio management, reporting, and trading.
Pricing: From $49/user/month. AI note-taker at an introductory $49/user/month. 14-day free trial available. The most transparent pricing in advisor technology.

Watch out for overlap: If your firm already uses Orion (which includes Redtail CRM), adding Wealthbox creates vendor redundancy. Evaluate whether the UX improvement justifies the additional cost and data synchronization work.
8. X1 Wealth (the coordination layer)

Best for: Advisors who have portfolio operations handled and need the layer above them: one shared record their clients and the other professionals all work from, so decisions, documents, and follow-through stop slipping between meetings.
Ideal firm size: Any firm serving complex households with multiple entities, multiple advisors, and planning needs beyond portfolio management.
What X1 does:

Orion, Black Diamond, Tamarac, and Addepar handle portfolio reporting. X1 carries the surrounding household context: the source documents, the decisions made from them, and the next step assigned to the right person.

One shared household record. You and the client see the same entities, documents, decisions, and Pulse telemetry. The client approves what leaves the household, while you add professional context to the record they already own. Every client household includes Pulse Black for multi-entity monitoring and its own VFO access.

Review Rooms. A bounded workspace for one approved professional packet. The household confirms the exact document set and intended recipient before X1 issues a revocable link; the professional can review that packet and return a response through the room.

Advisor Packets. Source-linked bundles of the client's snapshot, selected vault documents, and context. X1 prepares the proposed packet from the household record, and a person confirms the exact version before it is shared.

Review history. What was confirmed, which packet was shared, the professional's response, and who owns the next step. A confirmed outcome can be carried into the next review; customer-operated second-cycle proof is still required before calling that a retention moat.

Bring the client's data in. Import a client's Masttro or Addepar export, or read the statements they upload, and it lands in their register with the source on file. The connection is read-only, so the aggregator stays unchanged.
The why, documented. Family Constitution, the Family Office Blueprint, and plain-English estate-plan summaries turn the numbers into context the family can actually read.
Pricing:

Advisor Pro is $499/month for 1 professional seat and 10 client households; Team is $899/month for 3 seats and 18 households; Practice is $1,499/month for 5 seats and 30 households. Additional households are $50/month and additional professional seats are $149/month. Custom enterprise pricing is available.
Limitations:

items: X1 works alongside Orion, Black Diamond, Tamarac, or Addepar, which continue to handle portfolio management, reporting, and trading.
The platform is newer than established portfolio tools. Evaluate current features against your specific needs.

blocks.text: Explore the advisor platform
What portfolio platforms don't cover

The platforms in this comparison cover some combination of portfolio management, reporting, trading, and CRM. Client work also creates decisions, document requests, and follow-up across the advisor, CPA, attorney, and household. Those handoffs often sit outside the portfolio stack.
Governance and values

Families still need a place to articulate the principles behind financial decisions and agree on how major choices get made. Advisors often assemble that work in documents and meeting notes alongside the portfolio system.
Decision memory

When a client asks, "Why did we make that change two years ago?" the answer may be spread across CRM notes, email, and a performance report. A useful decision history keeps the reasoning, the context at the time, and the outcome together.
Multi-advisor coordination

Complex households may work with a CPA, an estate attorney, a financial planner, and an insurance specialist. Each professional handles a different part of the work, while the household and lead advisor carry the handoffs between them.
Client-facing strategic documents

Performance reports answer one set of questions. Between meetings, clients may also need an advisor packet, an estate-plan summary, or a clear record of a family decision. Those deliverables pull from a wider set of sources and people.
If these handoffs are where your team loses time or context, evaluate the coordination layer alongside the portfolio platform. See how X1 fits with an advisor's existing stack.

blocks.text: Orion and Addepar are leading the AI race among the platforms themselves. Orion's Denali focuses on operational efficiency (faster reports, easier data access). Addepar's Addison focuses on analytical intelligence (portfolio queries with traceable answers). Both approaches have merit, and both will evolve significantly over the next 12 months.

The September 2026 arrival of Anthropic's plugin changes the frame. Rather than one platform adding an assistant, the assistant now reads several of these platforms at once: Orion, Addepar, Tamarac, Wealthbox, Wealth.com, Zocks, iCapital, MoneyGuide, and BlackRock all ship connectors inside Claude for Financial Advisors, and Schwab is announced. The plugin is for financial professionals, with RIAs as its stated audience, Anthropic says an Enterprise license is required, it holds no client data, and it writes back to the firm's CRM. X1 is not one of those partner connectors. Claude Enterprise supports admin-added custom connectors, so by the documented setup X1 can be mounted in the same workspace and supply the piece the firm's platforms do not hold: the household's own confirmed record. We have not tested the two together. We read the plugin's public source in Claude for Financial Advisors vs X1.
AI in advisor technology is still early. Many firms remain in evaluation, so ask each vendor to run a live demo with representative firm data before making AI a deciding factor.
Implementation reality check
Platform migrations can create broken reporting, confused workflows, and months of parallel systems. Implementation evidence deserves as much attention as the feature list.
What to do before signing

items: Inventory your data sources.
List every custodian, alternatives administrator, and private holding. Confirm coverage during the demo and put it in the contract.
Define householding rules.
What counts as a household? How do trusts, LLCs, and partnerships roll up? This decision drives reporting structure.
Lock reporting standards.
Performance methodology (TWR vs. IRR), benchmark selection, valuation frequency for illiquid assets. Disagreements here surface months into implementation.
Plan a parallel reporting period.
Run both old and new systems simultaneously before switching client-facing views. Budget 30 to 90 days minimum.
Assign a data hygiene owner.
Reconciliation, exception handling, and ongoing data quality need a permanent owner.
Evaluate the exit path.
How does data export work if you switch platforms in three years? What format, what timeline, what cost? Vendors rarely volunteer this information.

What to do in the next 30 days
If you are actively evaluating advisor technology, here is a concrete sequence.

items: Week 1: Classify your firm archetype.

Use the four archetypes above. Be honest about whether you want consolidation, HNW specialization, best-of-breed flexibility, or client engagement innovation. This narrows eight platforms to two or three.
Week 2: Request scoped demos.
Provide your data source inventory and specific use cases. Ask each vendor to show how they handle your custodians, entity structures, and reporting requirements.
Week 3: Run the hard questions.
Get pricing with implementation costs broken out, the exit path in writing, a migration timeline with milestones, and dated commitments for any roadmap feature that matters to the decision.
Week 4: Evaluate the gap.
After demos, list the work left outside each finalist. Governance frameworks, advisor coordination, and decision history may call for a separate evaluation.
