h1: Orion vs Black Diamond in 2026: Verdict for RIAs and HNW Firms

blocks.text: Orion vs Black Diamond in 2026: Verdict for RIAs and HNW Firms
One runs your whole operation, the other makes HNW clients feel understood. Compared on trading, reporting, portals, pricing, and real migration cost.
By Mat Silverstein · Updated Aug 10, 2026

Orion and Black Diamond represent two different philosophies for enterprise wealth management technology. Orion has built an all-in-one ecosystem (CRM, portfolio accounting, trading, planning, compliance) while Black Diamond focuses on best-in-class reporting and portfolio management for complex, high-net-worth situations.
This guide helps RIAs and wealth managers evaluate which platform architecture fits their practice, plus a short migration checklist and the questions to ask in demos.
Last reviewed: February 5, 2026.
Key takeaways

items: Orion is the better fit when you want one vendor to run most of the stack.
Black Diamond is the better fit when reporting quality and complex portfolios are the differentiator.
Implementation risk is less about features and more about data conversion + workflows.
Neither platform solves the “between meetings” problem: client-ready planning deliverables and decision memory.

blocks.text: Quick verdict

Choose Orion if: You want a unified platform that handles everything (CRM, portfolio accounting, trading, planning, and compliance) from one vendor. Orion's scale and broad integration ecosystem mean extensive integrations and ongoing development. Best for firms wanting to consolidate their tech stack.

Choose Black Diamond if: You serve ultra-high-net-worth clients or family offices with complex, multi-entity portfolios and alternative investments. Black Diamond's reporting and data aggregation are unmatched for sophisticated wealth situations. Best for firms where client presentation matters as much as back-office efficiency.

Consider X1 Wealth as a complement if: You want one record your clients and their other professionals all work from (the decisions, the source-backed holdings by entity, the documents) on top of what your operational platform already runs. Neither Orion nor Black Diamond keeps the decisions behind the numbers or coordinates across the professionals around the household.
Comparison at a glance
Decision framework: which platform fits your firm
Most “vs” comparisons get stuck in feature checklists. That’s not how these platform decisions go in the real world.
The hard part is choosing the operating model you want to run for the next 3-7 years: one vendor running most workflows, or a reporting-first core with best-of-breed integrations.
Archetype A: the all-in-one consolidator
Choose Orion-first when the firm goal is consolidation.
You’ll feel good about this choice if:

items: Your ops team wants fewer vendors to manage
You want trading, billing, reporting, and planning to share one workflow surface
You’re standardizing a repeatable “household operating system” across many advisors

blocks.text: You’ll feel bad about this choice if:

items: You need premium, highly bespoke client reporting as a primary differentiator
Your firm culture is “best-of-breed or nothing”

blocks.text: Archetype B: reporting-first for UHNW complexity
Choose Black Diamond-first when client presentation quality and portfolio complexity are the competitive edge.
You’ll feel good about this choice if:

items: You live in multi-entity households (trusts, LLCs, foundations)
Alternatives and illiquid holdings are a daily reality
You’re willing to integrate CRM/planning/trading around the reporting core

blocks.text: You’ll feel bad about this choice if:

items: You want one vendor to own most workflows end-to-end
You don’t have an ops owner for integrations and data hygiene

blocks.text: Archetype C: best-of-breed integrator
If neither Orion nor Black Diamond feels like “the whole answer,” that’s normal. Many firms pick a core, then choose best-of-breed for planning, CRM, or specialty reporting.
If that’s you, prioritize:

items: Integration compatibility with your custodians + data providers
Clear reporting standards (householding rules, classification, performance methodology)
A migration plan that includes a parallel run period

blocks.text: Understanding Orion

Orion has grown from a portfolio accounting platform into a comprehensive wealth technology ecosystem. Through acquisitions (Redtail CRM, HiddenLevers risk analytics, Brinker Capital) and internal development, Orion now offers an all-in-one solution that can power an entire RIA's operations.
Orion's scale and market position

Key strengths
1. All-in-one ecosystem
Orion's value proposition is consolidation. One vendor for:

items: Portfolio accounting and reporting
CRM (Redtail integration)
Financial planning (Orion Planning)
Trading and rebalancing (Eclipse platform)
Compliance management
Risk analytics (HiddenLevers)
Client portal and mobile app

blocks.text: 2. Trading excellence

Eclipse, Orion's trading and rebalancing engine, is considered industry-leading. Household trading, tax-loss harvesting, asset category groupings, and sophisticated rebalancing rules give advisors institutional-grade execution.
3. Continuous innovation

Tax-aware, personalized portfolios at scale combining custom indexing with model portfolios
Meeting prep automation:

blocks.text: Understanding Black Diamond

Black Diamond, owned by SS&C Technologies (through Advent), takes a different approach: be the best at portfolio reporting and client communication for complex wealth situations. Rather than building everything, Black Diamond excels at its core and integrates with best-of-breed solutions for other needs.
Key strengths
1. Premium reporting and visualization

Black Diamond's reports are consistently rated as the most visually appealing and client-friendly in the industry. For firms where client presentation matters, especially with HNW clients who expect premium everything, this differentiation matters.
2. Alternative asset excellence

Family offices and UHNW clients have complex portfolios: private equity, hedge funds, real estate, art, collectibles. Black Diamond's data aggregation and alternative asset servicing handles these better than most competitors.
3. Multi-entity complexity
Trusts, LLCs, family limited partnerships, foundations: wealthy families have complicated structures. Black Diamond is built for this complexity, providing consolidated reporting across entities.
4. Client portal quality
The Black Diamond client portal is highly rated, offering:

items: Configurable dashboards with performance, income projections, allocations
Two-way secure document vault
Outside account aggregation for complete net worth view
Balance sheet reporting

blocks.text: 5. Integration ecosystem
Black Diamond is designed to sit in the middle of a broader tech stack. In practice, that means integrating CRM, planning, trading, and data workflows around the reporting core.
Black Diamond pricing

Black Diamond pricing is quote-driven. It’s commonly structured around firm scale (often AUM-based) plus the modules and services you need. Treat any “1 bp” rule-of-thumb pricing you hear as a starting point for budgeting, not a quote.

Black Diamond limitations

items: No native CRM:
Must integrate with Salesforce, Redtail, or others
No native financial planning:
Must integrate with eMoney, RightCapital, etc.
Implementation time:
3-6 months for firms under $1B AUM, 6-9 months for larger

blocks.text: Feature-by-feature breakdown
Portfolio accounting
Orion: Comprehensive portfolio accounting with sophisticated multi-currency, multi-custodian support. The Eclipse trading engine is tightly integrated.
Black Diamond: Strong portfolio accounting focused on complex wealth situations: alternatives, multi-entity structures, illiquid assets.
Winner: Tie. Orion for trading integration, Black Diamond for complexity handling.
Reporting
Orion: Robust reporting with customization options. Functional and comprehensive, if not always visually stunning.
Black Diamond: Premium, visually appealing reports designed to impress sophisticated clients. This is Black Diamond's core differentiator.
Winner: Black Diamond for client-facing presentation quality.
Trading and rebalancing
Orion: Eclipse is industry-leading. Household trading, tax-loss harvesting, model management, and sophisticated rebalancing at scale.
Black Diamond: Capable trading and rebalancing, but not the platform's primary focus.
Winner: Orion, clearly.
CRM
Orion: Redtail CRM included (with discount) or integrate alternatives. Tight workflow integration across the platform.
Black Diamond: No native CRM. Integrates with Salesforce, Redtail, Wealthbox, and others.
Winner: Orion for included functionality.
Financial planning
Orion: Orion Planning provides native planning capabilities. Also integrates with RightCapital, eMoney, MoneyGuidePro.
Black Diamond: No native planning. Integrates with major planning platforms.
Winner: Orion for included functionality.
Client portal
Orion: Solid client portal with mobile app. Performance views, document sharing, account aggregation.
Black Diamond: Highly rated portal with configurable dashboards, document vault, and detailed balance sheet reporting.
Winner: Black Diamond for portal quality and customization.
Alternative investments
Orion: Good alternative asset support that has improved significantly.
Black Diamond: Excellent alternative data aggregation and servicing, a core strength for family office work.
Winner: Black Diamond for complex alternative portfolios.
Implementation
Orion: Typically 3-6 months depending on firm complexity and which modules are implemented.
Black Diamond: 3-6 months for firms under $1B AUM, 6-9 months for larger firms.
Winner: Comparable, though Orion's modular approach may allow faster partial implementations.
Implementation and migration checklist (what to do before you sign)
If you’re migrating platforms, the biggest risk isn’t “missing a feature.” It’s broken reporting, confused workflows, and loss of trust with clients.
Use this checklist to reduce implementation surprises:

items: Inventory your stack.
Custodians, data feeds, CRM, planning, billing, trading, portals, data warehouse.
Define householding rules.
What counts as a household? How do entities roll up? Who owns classification?
Lock reporting standards.
Performance methodology, benchmarks, private asset valuations, fee treatment.
Run a parallel reporting period.
Compare old vs new outputs for a full cycle before you switch client-facing views.
Validate alternatives handling.
Who maintains private holdings, capital calls, and valuations? Our
capital call notice checklist
shows the fields worth capturing from each notice.
Train to workflows, not buttons.
Create a “day in the life” for ops + advisors and rehearse it.
Decide what the client sees.
Portal rollout plan, communication timeline, and who answers questions.

blocks.text: Pricing and contracts (what to ask in demos)
Neither Orion nor Black Diamond is priced like a consumer app. Most firms end up with a quote that reflects scope, services, and complexity.
Questions to ask before you sign:

items: What’s included in implementation vs billed separately?
What does data conversion cover (custodians, alternatives, historical performance)?
What are the required modules for “table stakes” workflows at your firm?
How do breakpoints work as you scale AUM or number of households?
What happens at renewal (contract length, uplift limits, support tiers)?

blocks.text: Who should choose Orion?
Orion is right for you if:

items: You want to consolidate multiple vendors into one platform
Trading and rebalancing efficiency is a priority
You value having CRM, planning, and compliance from one vendor
You serve a range of client types (not exclusively UHNW)
Integration ecosystem breadth matters for your tech stack
You're comfortable with a steeper learning curve for comprehensive features

blocks.text: Ideal Orion firm: A growing RIA with $200M-$2B AUM that wants operational efficiency through consolidation, values trading capabilities, and serves a diverse client base.
Who should choose Black Diamond?
Black Diamond is right for you if:

items: Client-facing reporting quality is a competitive differentiator
You serve UHNW clients and family offices with complex situations
Alternative investments are significant in client portfolios
Multi-entity structures (trusts, LLCs, foundations) are common
You already have preferred CRM and planning tools
Premium presentation matters to your client base

blocks.text: Ideal Black Diamond firm: A wealth manager serving $5M+ clients with complex portfolios, multiple entities, and alternative investments, where sophisticated reporting justifies premium positioning.
What neither platform offers
Both Orion and Black Diamond focus on advisor operations, the back-office efficiency that helps firms scale. But neither addresses what clients increasingly expect from their wealth relationships:
Values-based planning
Neither platform helps you document what clients actually care about: their family values, decision-making frameworks, or legacy intentions. You're left building these deliverables manually.
Governance frameworks
For wealthy families, governance is critical: How do they make financial decisions together? What's the process for major choices? Neither platform provides these frameworks.
Estate plan analysis
Clients have trusts and estate documents they don't understand. Neither Orion nor Black Diamond helps them (or you) make sense of these critical documents.
Client-ready strategic documents
Both platforms produce reports. But what do you hand clients between meetings that helps them understand their wealth strategy beyond performance numbers?

blocks.text: X1 Wealth: the coordination layer

X1 does not compete with Orion or Black Diamond for portfolio accounting or advisor operations. Both are excellent at what they do. X1 is the coordination layer above them, where you and your client work from one household record.

One shared household record: the decisions behind the numbers (what was decided, why, who owns the next step), a source-backed register of what the household owns by entity, plus the documents and Pulse telemetry, all in one place you and the client both work from. Import a client's reporting export, or read the statements they upload, and it lands in the register with the source on file.

Decision Memory: a running record of what was decided and why, with follow-up checkpoints to revisit it. The reasoning a reporting or accounting platform never keeps. And it compounds: every review and decision deepens a record an operational platform cannot rebuild from its reports.
Advisor Packets: source-linked bundles of the client's snapshot, documents, and context that prep the client and their other professionals for a meeting.
The why, documented: Family Constitution, the Family Office Blueprint, and plain-English estate-plan summaries turn the numbers into context the family can actually read.
Best for: Advisors using Orion or Black Diamond who want the coordination layer above their operational stack, without building it from scratch.

blocks.text: RightCapital vs eMoney: Financial Planning Software for Advisors in 2026

By Mat Silverstein · Updated Jun 18, 2026

RightCapital and eMoney are two of the most popular financial planning software platforms for advisors, but they serve different practices. RightCapital offers modern UX, faster onboarding, and transparent pricing that works for solo advisors and growing RIAs. eMoney provides the deepest planning engine available, essential for complex wealth situations, but at enterprise pricing.
This guide helps you choose the right platform for your practice, and explores how client-facing tools like X1 Wealth can complement your planning software.
Last reviewed: February 5, 2026.
Key takeaways

items: RightCapital is usually the faster path to usable, client-facing plans for solo advisors and growing RIAs.
eMoney is usually the better fit when you need the deepest scenario modeling and edge-case coverage.
The real risk isn’t features. It’s onboarding workflows, data hygiene, and client portal rollout.
Neither platform solves qualitative planning (values, governance, decision memory) without extra work.

blocks.text: Quick verdict

Choose RightCapital if: You're a solo advisor or small RIA who wants comprehensive planning without a steep learning curve. RightCapital’s modern UX and guided workflows tend to get teams to “usable in meetings” faster.

Choose eMoney if: You serve ultra-high-net-worth clients with complex needs like multigenerational trusts, stock option exercises, or state tax arbitrage. eMoney's projection engine is unmatched for these scenarios, and larger firms often get discounted rates through broker-dealer relationships.

Consider X1 Wealth as a complement if: You want one record your clients and their other professionals all work from (the decisions, the source-backed holdings by entity, the documents, the soft-side governance) around the plan your modeling software produces. Neither RightCapital nor eMoney keeps the decisions behind the plan or coordinates across the professionals around the household.
Comparison at a glance
Decision framework: which platform fits your practice
Financial planning software decisions are rarely about “the best tool.” They’re about the operating model you want to run.
Archetype A: solo advisor or small RIA (speed wins)
Choose RightCapital-first when:

items: You want fast onboarding and high advisor adoption
You need a clean client portal and visual planning outputs
You’d rather spend time on clients than on training

items: Over-customizing early. Get to a repeatable planning workflow first, then refine.

Choose eMoney-first when:

items: You routinely model trusts, equity comp, multi-entity structures, and “weird” scenarios
You need depth and control more than you need a modern UI
Your clients (and team) expect enterprise-grade planning systems

blocks.text: Understanding RightCapital

Founded in 2015, RightCapital has become the fastest-growing financial planning software by focusing on user experience. The platform was built with modern technology from the ground up, resulting in faster updates and a more responsive interface than legacy systems.
Key strengths
1. Intuitive data entry
RightCapital’s guided workflow minimizes missed details that can throw off projections. The typical advantage is time-to-adoption: teams get to usable outputs quickly.
2. Visual presentation tools

blocks.text: 3. Modern client portal

4. Transparent pricing

blocks.text: Understanding eMoney

eMoney has been the industry standard since 2000, and Fidelity's 2015 acquisition cemented its position as the enterprise choice. With 138,000+ users serving 7 million households, eMoney offers the deepest planning capabilities available.
Key strengths
1. Unmatched projection depth
eMoney handles scenarios no other platform can:

items: Trust distributions with complex terms

Stock option exercise strategies

Multi-entity business structures

blocks.text: 2. Decision Center
Real-time "what-if" modeling that lets advisors toggle assumptions and show clients the impact on net worth instantly. This collaborative feature is particularly effective in client meetings.
3. Client alerts and monitoring
eMoney's "feed" keeps advisors updated with financial alerts, news, and real-time data related to their clients, proactive rather than reactive.
4. Enterprise integrations
For larger firms needing fully open APIs and deep custodial connections, eMoney remains the standard.
eMoney pricing

blocks.text: Feature-by-feature breakdown
Ease of use

eMoney: Typically deeper and more complex. Teams often need a more structured onboarding and training plan.

eMoney: Decision Center allows real-time scenario modeling in meetings. Reports are comprehensive but more traditional in design.

Mobile experience

eMoney: iOS and Android apps available, supporting on-the-go access.

User satisfaction
Both platforms are widely used. In practice, this decision is often less about “ratings” and more about which platform your team will consistently use with clients.
Winner: The one your team adopts.

RightCapital is right for you if:

items: You're a solo advisor or small RIA

What neither platform offers

Both RightCapital and eMoney excel at financial projections, modeling cash flows, retirement scenarios, and investment outcomes. But neither addresses the qualitative planning that high-net-worth families increasingly expect:
Values-based planning
Neither platform helps you document what clients actually care about: their family values, decision-making frameworks, or legacy intentions. You're left doing this on paper or not at all.
Family governance
For clients with $2M+ net worth, family governance becomes critical: How do they make financial decisions together? What's their investment philosophy? Neither tool provides frameworks.
Client-ready deliverables
RightCapital and eMoney produce advisor-facing plans. But what do you hand clients between meetings? What documents help them communicate with their CPA or estate attorney?
Estate document analysis
Clients have trusts and estate documents they don't understand. Neither platform helps them, or you, make sense of what they've already paid attorneys to create.

blocks.text: Tamarac vs Black Diamond (2026): An RIA Buyer's Guide
Tamarac and Black Diamond compared for RIAs: portfolio operations, reporting, CRM, client experience, implementation risk, pricing, and an RFP scorecard.
By Mat Silverstein · Updated Aug 9, 2026

Tamarac is the stronger fit for an RIA that wants tightly connected trading, rebalancing, reporting, billing, CRM, proposals, and UMA workflows. Black Diamond is the stronger fit when polished client reporting, complex household views, alternative assets, and a broad wealth-management ecosystem carry more weight. The right answer depends on how your firm actually works, not which demo has more features.
Last reviewed: August 9, 2026.
Quick verdict
Choose Envestnet Tamarac when portfolio operations are the center of the decision and the firm wants trading, rebalancing, reporting, billing, CRM, and client access designed as one RIA workflow.

Choose SS&C Black Diamond Wealth Solutions when the client and reporting experience is the center of the decision, especially for HNW and UHNW households with multiple entities, outside assets, and alternative investments.
Both are enterprise purchases. Neither company publishes enough standard pricing for a dependable online cost comparison.
A quick self-check
Start with the work that is hardest today.

items: Does the trading team live in side files and manual checks?
Do clients complain about reports or the portal?
Are billing rules hard to explain and correct?
Do private assets break the household view?
Does the firm want one main vendor or several focused tools?
Who will own the new system after launch?

blocks.text: If trading and portfolio work cause the pain, start with Tamarac. If client reporting causes the pain, start with Black Diamond. Bring the people who do the work into both demos.
Tamarac vs Black Diamond at a glance

head: Decision
Tamarac
Black Diamond
rows: Reporting-led wealth firm, HNW/UHNW client experience
Trading, reporting, billing, CRM, portal, proposals, UMA
Portfolio reporting, portal, CRM, trading, compliance, trust and investment services
Available within the unified Black Diamond suite
Validate workflow depth with your actual assets
Strong fit for complex household reporting; test data collection separately
Converting portfolio rules and operating workflows
Household data, report definitions, integrations, and scope across SS&C products

blocks.text: Why this comparison is hard to find online

Google's first page for this query is mostly forum threads, broad platform roundups, and pages comparing one of these products with somebody else. That leaves buyers with opinions but little structure.

The useful comparison is not “does it have a portal?” Both do. The useful comparison is whether the software can reproduce your firm's hardest work without creating a permanent layer of manual cleanup.
Where Tamarac is stronger
Portfolio operations as one workflow

Tamarac's official product page describes an end-to-end suite covering trading and rebalancing, performance reporting, billing, CRM, a client portal, proposals, and unified managed accounts. That operating focus is its clearest advantage.

For an RIA that manages models across many households, the buying question is often operational: can the team make a change, respect account and tax constraints, execute it, bill correctly, and explain the result without moving data through several disconnected systems?
A system built specifically for RIAs

Envestnet says Tamarac has served RIAs for more than 25 years. Its 2026 release materials show continued investment in trading access during synchronization, security reserves, reporting controls, portal improvements, CRM automation, and MoneyGuide connections.
Those details matter more than a generic “all-in-one” label. Ask Tamarac to show your operations team the before, during, and after states of one real workflow.
Where Black Diamond is stronger
Client-facing reporting

Black Diamond built its reputation around portfolio reporting and the client experience. SS&C now presents Black Diamond as a wider wealth solutions suite, but reporting remains the reason many firms put it on the shortlist.

For firms serving complex households, the test is whether an advisor can move from a consolidated family view to the underlying account, entity, manager, or asset without losing the story. Bring a difficult household to the demo, not a clean sample account.
Breadth across SS&C

SS&C unified its wealth offerings under Black Diamond Wealth Solutions in 2025. The company says the suite now serves more than 3,000 firms, 800,000 active users, and $3.6 trillion in assets, with capabilities spanning reporting, alternatives, portal, CRM, trust, retirement, compliance, investment management, trading, rebalancing, billing, and business intelligence.

Those are vendor-reported figures. The practical benefit is access to a broader set of services. The corresponding risk is scope: buyers need to know which product, team, contract, and support path owns each promised workflow.
The six-case demo that reveals the real difference
Give both vendors the same cases at least a week before the demo.

items: A restricted household trade.
Include legacy positions, cash needs, tax constraints, and one account that cannot follow the model.
A messy household report.
Include trusts, LLCs, held-away assets, a private fund, and two people who need different views.
A fee correction.
Change a householding or billing rule and trace the downstream effect.
A client request.
Upload a document, update the record, notify the team, and show what the client sees.
A data break.
Simulate a missing feed or incorrect classification and show the review trail.
A new relationship.
Move from proposal to opened accounts and the first client report.

blocks.text: Score the result on manual steps, clarity, reviewer controls, data lineage, and time. Have the people who will operate the system score it separately from the executives who will buy it.
Implementation and migration risk
The winning demo is not necessarily the safer migration. Ask both vendors for a written plan covering:

items: historical data and performance conversion;
household, entity, security, and account mapping;
model, restriction, billing, and report configuration;
custodian and third-party integrations;
parallel-run reconciliation;
staff training and post-launch support;
data export and termination assistance.

blocks.text: Then choose a representative migration cohort. It should include ordinary households and the awkward exceptions that consume operations time. A platform that handles the clean 80% but makes the difficult 20% worse has not solved the problem.
Pricing: compare the three-year operating cost

Tamarac and Black Diamond use custom pricing. Ask for one worksheet that includes software, implementation, conversion, integrations, professional services, training, expected internal staffing, and annual increases.

Do not compare only the license quote. A cheaper platform can cost more if it requires more reconciliation, custom reporting, or vendor management. A more expensive platform can be justified if it retires other systems and manual work. Make both cases visible before the contract is signed.
Where X1 fits

X1 does not replace Tamarac or Black Diamond. Those systems manage portfolio operations and reporting. X1 keeps the household's planning context, source documents, decisions, and professional handoffs in a shared record around that core.
See the broader advisor platform comparison, compare Orion with Black Diamond, or read Tamarac vs Orion if suite consolidation is the main decision.
Browse every X1 comparison or see how X1 works with an advisor's existing stack.
Frequently asked questions
Is Tamarac a TAMP?

Tamarac is an RIA technology platform within Envestnet. Envestnet also provides investment-management and TAMP-related services, but buyers should confirm which services and contracts are actually included in a Tamarac proposal.
How much does Black Diamond cost?
SS&C does not publish a standard price sufficient for a reliable estimate. Cost depends on firm scope, assets, products, services, and implementation. Request an itemized three-year quote.
Which platform is better for alternatives?

Black Diamond is often shortlisted for complex household and alternative-asset reporting. Tamarac supports broad portfolio workflows. Test both with the exact private assets, data sources, valuation cadence, and documents your firm manages.
Can X1 replace Tamarac or Black Diamond?
No. X1 is a planning and professional-coordination layer, not portfolio accounting, trading, billing, or performance-reporting software.

blocks.text: Tamarac vs Orion (2026): Which RIA Platform Should You Choose?
Compare Tamarac and Orion for trading, reporting, CRM, planning, AI, integrations, implementation, and pricing. Includes a practical RIA demo scorecard.
By Mat Silverstein · Updated Aug 9, 2026

Tamarac and Orion are both broad RIA platforms. Tamarac is the stronger fit when the firm wants portfolio trading, reporting, billing, CRM, proposals, and UMA workflows centered in the Envestnet ecosystem. Orion is the stronger fit when the firm wants a wider connected suite with Redtail CRM, planning, portfolio accounting, Eclipse trading, risk, compliance, and Denali AI. The best choice is the one that removes the most expensive handoffs in your practice.
Last reviewed: August 9, 2026.
Quick verdict
Choose Tamarac when investment operations are the organizing center of your firm and Envestnet's portfolio, proposal, and managed-account ecosystem fits the way you want to scale.
Choose Orion when you want a broad advisor technology suite, a large integration network, and an AI roadmap that connects CRM, planning, portfolio, and risk data.
This is a close comparison. Both vendors can cover many of the same category labels. Your decision should come from completed workflows, not a row of checkmarks.
A quick self-check
Answer these questions with your operations lead.

items: Which system does the team open first each morning?
Which manual handoff causes the most rework?
Does the firm already depend on Envestnet or Orion products?
Which tools could a new platform truly remove?
Who will maintain models, data rules, and reports?
How hard would it be to leave the new system later?

blocks.text: The answers should shape the demo. A long feature list should not.

Pick one lead for the search. Ask staff for three hard cases. Remove all client names. Give each firm the same data. Use the same time limit. Count each handoff. Count each manual fix. Save every open question. Score the work before price. Then compare the full cost.
Tamarac vs Orion at a glance

head: Decision
Tamarac
Orion
rows: Trading, rebalancing, reporting, billing, CRM, portal, proposals, UMA
CRM, planning, portfolio accounting, trading, compliance, risk, reporting

Integrates with MoneyGuide and Envestnet tools
Evaluate current workflow-level features in demo
Denali AI spans embedded, packaged, and enterprise offerings
Product overlap, suite complexity, and lock-in

blocks.text: The real choice: which ecosystem should own the workflow?

Tamarac versus Orion is not a point-solution decision. It is an architectural decision. Whichever platform wins will influence data definitions, staff training, integrations, reporting, and the firm's next several software purchases.
That is why the question “which has more features?” is weak. Both have many. Ask instead:

items: Which platform can complete our ten most common workflows with the fewest manual handoffs?
Which platform handles our exceptions without creating a spreadsheet shadow system?
Which ecosystem contains the products we actually want, rather than products we would tolerate for a bundle?
Which vendor gives us a credible data export and exit path?

blocks.text: Where Tamarac is stronger
An RIA operations center

Tamarac's current product materials describe connected trading and rebalancing, reporting, billing, CRM, client portal, proposal, and UMA capabilities. This is compelling when the investment operations team wants those jobs to share one set of workflows and portfolio data.
The platform is especially relevant for RIAs already using Envestnet services or planning to build around them. The value comes from the system around Tamarac, not only the reporting screen.
Recent operational improvements

Envestnet's May 2026 update describes trading access during synchronization, security reserves, new Report Studio controls, client portal changes, bulk document handling, CRM automation, and deeper MoneyGuide goal visibility. Those are practical operating details. Ask the vendor to demonstrate which are generally available in your proposed configuration.
Where Orion is stronger
Breadth and integration reach

Orion describes a 12-product advisor platform spanning CRM, planning, portfolio accounting, trading, compliance, risk, billing, reporting, and client experience. It also says the platform connects with more than 100 partners.
That gives Orion a strong consolidation case. A firm can standardize around Orion without assuming every specialized need must come from an outside vendor.
Denali AI across the stack

Orion's Denali AI is designed to work across its connected data and product environment. The official page emphasizes firm-isolated data and review by financial professionals. That is more useful than a generic chatbot if the assistant can retrieve the right client context and leave a reviewable trail.
Still, buy the workflow, not the label. Ask Orion to complete a current task your team performs manually and show every source, permission, review step, and saved output.
The head-to-head demo script
Use the same script with both vendors and prohibit canned sample data for at least half of it.

head: Workflow
What the team should prove
rows: Proposal, account setup, household rules, client portal, first report
Restrictions, tax concerns, cash, trade review, execution, documentation
Planning, performance, open service items, and client-ready output
Correct a rule, approve it, and trace the result
Detect a broken feed or classification, assign it, correct it, preserve history
Move a task from advisor to operations without email or a side spreadsheet

blocks.text: Have each evaluator record the number of screens, manual entries, waits, and unresolved questions. That record is more useful than a 200-row feature matrix.
Integration and exit risk
An “all-in-one” platform can reduce daily friction while increasing switching cost. That trade can be sensible, but it should be explicit.
Before signing, require answers to these questions:

items: Which system is authoritative for client, household, account, security, model, and document data?
Which integrations are real-time, vendor-supported, and included in the quote?
What happens when an integration fails?
Can the firm export data in usable fields, with history and identifiers intact?
Which custom configurations can be carried forward after a contract ends?
How much professional-services work is required for a change after launch?

blocks.text: Pricing and implementation

Neither vendor publishes a standard price that supports a fair online comparison. Ask for a three-year total that includes implementation, conversion, integrations, training, support tier, optional products, and expected increases.

Then price internal effort. Count the people needed for implementation, the work paused during conversion, and the recurring manual steps left after launch. Software price is only one line in the decision.
Where X1 fits

X1 does not replace Tamarac or Orion. They run portfolio and practice workflows. X1 organizes the household's planning context, source documents, decisions, and coordination with the other professionals around the client.
For adjacent decisions, see Tamarac vs Black Diamond, Orion vs Black Diamond, and the full advisor platform comparison.

Frequently asked questions
Who typically uses Orion?
Orion serves RIAs, wealth managers, enterprise firms, and asset managers that need connected advisor, portfolio, trading, planning, compliance, and reporting technology.
Is Tamarac only for large firms?
Tamarac is commonly evaluated by established RIAs with meaningful operations needs. Fit depends more on workflow complexity, staffing, and the Envestnet relationship than on a single asset threshold.
Which has better integrations?

Orion publicly states that its open platform connects with more than 100 partners. Tamarac offers integrations within and beyond Envestnet. Buyers should compare the exact custodians and products they use, including ownership and support when a connection breaks.
Can X1 replace Tamarac or Orion?
No. X1 complements RIA operating platforms with household planning context and professional coordination. It is not trading, billing, portfolio accounting, or performance-reporting software.

blocks.text: Wealth.com vs Vanilla (2026): Estate Planning Software Compared
Compare Wealth.com and Vanilla for advisor-led estate planning: document creation, plan review, scenario modeling, client experience, implementation, and pricing.
By Mat Silverstein · Updated Sep 15, 2026

Wealth.com is the stronger fit for firms that want a broad, connected estate-planning workflow, including document review, document creation, diagrams, reports, tasks, and a client vault. Vanilla is the stronger fit when the advisor's priority is visual estate analysis, advanced strategy modeling, and side-by-side client scenarios. The products overlap, so the decision should come from a real household case and a clear attorney-review process.
Last reviewed: September 15, 2026.
Quick verdict

Choose Wealth.com when you want one estate-planning environment that moves from existing-document analysis to new-document creation, client reporting, task management, and ongoing plan administration.
Choose Vanilla when your team wins by making estate structures understandable and comparing advanced planning scenarios with clients before legal documents are drafted.
Keep both on the shortlist if estate planning is a signature service. The center of gravity differs, but neither vendor stays inside a narrow feature box anymore.
A quick self-check
Ask what your firm wants to make easier.

items: Is the first problem reading old plans?
Is the first problem showing clients how the plan works?
Do advisors need to compare advanced strategies?
Does the firm want to prepare new documents in the same system?
Who gives legal advice and approves the final documents?
Who checks that trusts are funded and forms are updated?

blocks.text: The last two questions matter most. A clear diagram is useful. A clear handoff is what gets the plan finished.
Wealth.com vs Vanilla at a glance

head: Decision
Wealth.com
Vanilla
rows: Visual analysis and advanced scenario modeling

blocks.text: The boundary that matters most

Estate planning software can help an advisor find issues, explain structures, model choices, gather information, and prepare documents. It does not erase the distinction between financial planning and legal advice.
Before choosing either product, write down who is responsible for each step:

items: gathering household and beneficiary facts;
reading and summarizing existing documents;
identifying questions worth reviewing;
modeling possible planning structures;
providing legal advice;
drafting or approving legal documents;
signing, witnessing, and notarizing;
funding trusts and changing titles or beneficiaries;
checking that the plan still matches the household later.

blocks.text: If the vendor demo does not make those handoffs clear, the feature set is not the main problem.
Where Wealth.com is stronger
A broad estate-planning workflow

Wealth.com's current platform pages present a connected set of tools: Ester AI for document extraction and summaries, document creation, a Scenario Builder, Report Builder, Estate Flow diagrams, a balance sheet, a document vault, Heritage Map, and Task Center.

That breadth is useful for firms that want estate planning to be a repeatable service rather than an occasional referral. The platform can help organize what exists, show how the plan works, prepare new documents where appropriate, and keep follow-through visible.
From analysis to administration

The Task Center and vault matter because estate work often fails after the strategy discussion. A signed trust that was never funded or a beneficiary form that was never updated can leave the household with a plan that looks finished but is not operational.
In the demo, ask Wealth.com to take one issue all the way from a source document to a completed and verified task. Do not accept a tour of disconnected screens.
Where Vanilla is stronger
Visual estate understanding

Vanilla is built around helping advisors and clients see an estate plan. Its public materials emphasize Estate Health Check, V/AI, Document Builder, and visual diagrams that make ownership and transfer paths easier to discuss.
That is valuable when the advisor's first job is turning a folder of documents into a conversation the client can follow.
Advanced scenario modeling

Vanilla's Scenarios product is designed to model and compare estate strategies, including techniques such as GRATs, SLATs, and charitable planning. Its product materials describe quick-add and full-balance-sheet approaches, side-by-side results, and client-ready deliverables.

This can be a meaningful advantage for advisors serving households where the planning conversation involves multiple structures and trade-offs. The output is still a planning model, not a substitute for legal and tax review.
The case-study demo both vendors should complete
Use one anonymized household with enough complexity to reveal the workflow:

items: a revocable trust and one irrevocable trust;
a business interest and two pieces of real estate;
retirement accounts and life insurance;
inconsistent beneficiary information;
an old power of attorney;
a charitable goal;
a possible advanced gifting strategy;
a CPA and estate attorney who need different follow-ups.

blocks.text: Ask each vendor to:

items: ingest the existing documents;
show every extracted fact with its source;
identify conflicts and missing information;
diagram the current plan;
model one proposed change;
produce the client explanation;
assign the professional handoffs;
show how completion and trust funding are verified;
revisit the plan after a business sale or family change.

blocks.text: The platform that produces the clearest, safest workflow for your team is a better fit than the platform with the longest feature page.
Pricing and contract questions
Neither vendor publishes a standard price that is sufficient for a dependable comparison. Request a complete quote and ask:

items: Is pricing based on advisors, households, plans, documents, or firm size?
Which document types and jurisdictions are included?
Is attorney review included, optional, or the firm's responsibility?
Are advanced scenarios included in the base package?
What happens to client documents and diagrams if the firm leaves?
Are implementation, training, and data migration separate charges?

blocks.text: Where X1 fits

X1 offers estate-document review for households and advisors, connected to the household's source documents and professional follow-through. That makes it another option for reviewing an existing plan, not an established replacement for either vendor's full modeling or document-creation suite.

Updated September 5, 2026: our FP Alpha vs Wealth.com guide compares estate review and tax planning separately, with a clearly scoped X1 section. X1 publishes these comparisons and offers its own review tools.

Updated September 15, 2026: Wealth.com is the estate and tax launch partner inside Anthropic's Claude for Financial Advisors, a plugin for RIAs on Claude Enterprise whose estate and tax brief reads the Wealth.com plan and cross-checks it against account titling and beneficiaries. That is an advisor-side capability; the household still reaches Wealth.com only through an advisor. X1's estate review runs for the household directly and compares the reviewed plan to the household's own entities, accounts, policies, and beneficiary facts. See Claude for Financial Advisors vs X1.
See the estate plan review checklist, the document-backed planning guide, or the broader advisor software comparison.
Browse every X1 comparison or see how X1 works with an advisor's existing stack.
Frequently asked questions
Is Wealth.com legitimate estate planning software?

Wealth.com is an estate-planning platform for advisors and wealth firms. Buyers should still evaluate security, legal workflow, jurisdiction coverage, attorney involvement, contract terms, and client fit.
Does Vanilla draft estate documents?
Vanilla includes Document Builder alongside its analysis and scenario tools. Confirm the specific document types, jurisdictions, review process, and professional responsibilities in your proposal.
Which is better for advanced estate strategies?

Vanilla has a strong public story around visual side-by-side scenario modeling. Wealth.com also offers scenario tools within a broader estate workflow. Test both with the same household and planning question.
Does either platform replace an estate attorney?
No. Software can support analysis, education, document workflows, and coordination. The household should use qualified legal and tax professionals for advice and review appropriate to its situation.

By Mat Silverstein · Updated Jun 18, 2026

Wealth Factory is a financial coaching company that's been serving entrepreneurs since the mid 2010s. But if you're researching alternatives, whether due to pricing concerns, mixed reviews, or simply wanting to explore options, this guide covers the landscape of financial education and coaching for high-income business owners.
Last reviewed: February 5, 2026.
Disclosure

X1 Wealth's founder was a co-founder of Wealth Factory until 2023. This comparison reflects our honest assessment of the current market landscape. We have no ongoing business relationship with Wealth Factory. Most of Wealth Factory's original co-founders are no longer involved with the company and have moved on to other ventures.
Key takeaways

items: Wealth Factory can be a fit if you want structured coaching and are comfortable with consultation-based pricing.
Many entrepreneurs look for alternatives when they want more transparency, more measurable outcomes, or fewer product-aligned incentives.
If you already have a CPA and attorney, the best “alternative” may be a visibility + coordination layer (so strategies actually get implemented).

operating model
: coaching, technology, or a hybrid.

blocks.text: If you're a current Wealth Factory client (and considering switching)

blocks.text: What is Wealth Factory?

Wealth Factory positions itself as a financial education and coaching company for entrepreneurs and high-income professionals. Their "Wealth Architecture" program combines training, coaching, and access to licensed professionals to help clients implement financial strategies.
What they offer:

items: Financial coaching
Life insurance product education
Cash flow optimization strategies

blocks.text: The coaching vs. technology decision
Here's the fundamental question: Do you need someone to tell you what to do, or do you need tools to help you do what you already know?
If this distinction is the real blocker, see our deeper guide on why financial coaching without technology is flying blind.

Coaching programs (Wealth Factory, Multiplier, Strategic Coach) provide frameworks, accountability, and expert guidance. They're valuable when you don't know what you don't know, or when you need external accountability to implement.
Technology platforms (X1 Wealth) provide tools, insights, and recommendations. They're valuable when you're capable of implementation but need better information and coordination.
The visibility gap in coaching-only programs
Here's what most coaching programs don't address: How do you know if the strategies are actually working?

You're relying on memory and scattered spreadsheets
There's no way to prove ROI on your coaching investment

blocks.text: It's like hiring a personal trainer but never tracking your workouts or stepping on a scale. You might be making progress, or you might be paying for expensive conversation.

The best setup for many entrepreneurs: Use both. A coaching program for strategic direction and accountability, plus technology for ongoing visibility and implementation tracking. This is why Multiplier includes X1 Wealth. The combination addresses both needs. The coaching tells you what to do; the technology shows you whether it's working.

h1: YNAB Alternatives for High Earners: Beyond Zero-Based Budgeting in 2026

blocks.text: YNAB Alternatives for High Earners: Beyond Zero-Based Budgeting in 2026
When you've outgrown every-dollar tracking, here are the budgeting apps that scale with high incomes, plus what to focus on once your budget runs itself.
By Mat Silverstein · Updated Jun 18, 2026

YNAB (You Need A Budget) is excellent for building financial discipline. Its zero-based methodology has helped millions escape the paycheck-to-paycheck cycle. But if your income comfortably exceeds your expenses and you’re still assigning every dollar to categories, you might be solving the wrong problem.
This guide covers YNAB alternatives that work better for high-income households, and what to focus on once your budget essentially runs itself.
Last reviewed: February 5, 2026.
Key takeaways

items: YNAB is strongest when you need a method that changes behavior.
Once budgeting is stable, the “next level” is visibility + strategy (net worth, taxes, estate, coordination).
High-maintenance workflows break; choose an app you’ll actually keep clean.
Don’t over-optimize categories when the bigger decisions are elsewhere.

blocks.text: The high-earner YNAB dilemma

Here’s the uncomfortable truth: when your income is high and your net worth is growing, the ROI of tracking every coffee purchase drops fast. The time you spend categorizing transactions is often better spent on:

items: Tax optimization
Equity compensation strategy (RSUs, options, ESPP)
Estate planning and wealth protection
Investment allocation across account types

blocks.text: YNAB solves behavior problems. But high earners typically don't have behavior problems. They have strategy problems.
That said, if you still want visibility into your spending (many do), here are the apps that work better for complex financial situations.
Best YNAB alternatives for high earners
1. Monarch Money: Best all-in-one financial dashboard
Pricing: $14.99/month or $99.99/year
Why high earners like it: Monarch tracks spending AND investments in one place. You get net worth monitoring, portfolio allocation views, and spending categorization without YNAB's rigid methodology.
Key features:

items: Investment tracking across all accounts (YNAB doesn't do this)
Flexible budgeting without strict zero-based rules
Unlimited shared access for couples (critical for dual-income households)
Automatic subscription detection
Three aggregators for better bank connectivity

blocks.text: The upgrade from YNAB: Skip the "give every dollar a job" ceremony. Set category limits once, monitor trends, and focus on bigger-picture optimization.
Best for: Dual-income households who want complete financial visibility without a strict zero-based workflow.
2. Copilot: Best for Apple users with variable income
Pricing: $13/month or $95/year
Why high earners like it: Copilot's AI categorization learns your patterns and handles variable income (bonuses, RSU vesting, commissions) better than rigid budgeting systems.
Key features:

items: Private AI model learns YOUR categorization preferences
Adaptive budgets that adjust based on actual behavior
Recurring transaction prediction (knows when bills hit)
Rebalancing feature that optimizes budget allocation
Beautiful native iOS/Mac/iPad apps

blocks.text: The upgrade from YNAB: Stop teaching a budgeting app the same categories every month. Copilot's AI handles it.
Best for: Apple-ecosystem professionals with bonus-heavy compensation who want minimal maintenance budgeting.
Limitation: iOS/Mac only, no Android or Windows.
3. Simplifi by Quicken: Best for straightforward tracking
Pricing: $5.99/month (billed annually at $71.88)

Why high earners like it: Simplifi is the simplest path from YNAB for people who just want expense tracking without zero-based budgeting. The "Planned Spend" feature works like YNAB without the philosophy.
Key features:

items: Zero-based "Planned Spend" feature for those who want it
Investment and net worth tracking
Bill calendar with upcoming payment alerts
Subscription monitoring
Watchlists for specific spending categories

blocks.text: The upgrade from YNAB: Similar structure, less ideology, lower price.
Best for: YNAB users who want continuity without the methodology.
4. PocketSmith: Best for long-term financial projections
Pricing: Free tier available; Premium at $9.95/month; Super at $19.95/month

Why high earners like it: PocketSmith forecasts your daily account balances up to 30 years into the future. For people planning FIRE (Financial Independence, Retire Early) or optimizing multi-year tax strategies, this visibility is valuable.
Key features:

items: 30-year financial forecasting
Multiple currency support (important for expats)
Calendar-based cash flow planning
What-if scenario modeling
International bank support

blocks.text: The upgrade from YNAB: Think decades, not months. Model the impact of decisions before making them.
Best for: FIRE-focused professionals or expats with international accounts.
5. Tiller Money: Best for spreadsheet people
Pricing: $79/year

Why high earners like it: Tiller automatically pulls transactions into Google Sheets or Excel, giving you complete control over your analysis. For data-obsessed high earners who want to build custom dashboards, nothing else comes close.
Key features:

items: Automatic daily transaction syncing to spreadsheets
Complete customization (it's just a spreadsheet)
Template library for different tracking styles
Works with any bank (via Plaid integration)
No mobile app, spreadsheet is the interface

blocks.text: The upgrade from YNAB: Build exactly what you want without app limitations.
Best for: Finance professionals who think in spreadsheets and want total control.
6. Empower Personal Dashboard: Best free option for tracking
Pricing: Free (wealth management services at 0.89%+ for $100k+ clients)

Why high earners like it: Empower's free dashboard offers the best net worth and investment tracking available. Yes, they'll try to sell you wealth management services, but the free tier is genuinely useful.
Key features:

items: Comprehensive investment tracking and analysis
Fee analyzer that finds hidden fund costs
Retirement planning projections
Net worth history with detailed breakdowns
Investment allocation analysis

blocks.text: The upgrade from YNAB: Get investment visibility YNAB doesn't offer. The spending tracking is secondary.
Best for: Anyone who wants free net worth tracking and can decline sales calls.
Trade-off: Expect calls from Empower advisors if you have $100k+ linked.
7. Actual Budget: Best open-source option
Pricing: Free (self-hosted) or ~$2/month (hosted options)
Why high earners like it: Actual is an open-source YNAB clone for people who want zero-based budgeting without the subscription. Your data stays on your own infrastructure.
Key features:

items: YNAB-style envelope budgeting
Local-first with optional sync
SimpleFIN integration for US bank connections
Complete data ownership
Active development community

blocks.text: The upgrade from YNAB: Same methodology, no subscription, full data control.
Best for: Privacy-conscious users who are comfortable with self-hosting.
Quick comparison
What high earners should actually focus on
Here's the uncomfortable truth about budgeting apps: once your income exceeds your spending by a comfortable margin, tracking where money goes matters less than optimizing where money grows.
Tax optimization (worth $10k-$50k+ annually)
At $300k+ income, the difference between mediocre and excellent tax strategy can be $50k annually:

items: S-corp election for business income:
saves 15.3% on reasonable salary portion
Mega backdoor Roth contributions:
up to $70,500 additional Roth space
Tax-loss harvesting:
automated in taxable accounts
Asset location optimization:
right investments in right account types
Qualified Small Business Stock (QSBS):
$10M federal exclusion if you qualify

blocks.text: No budgeting app surfaces these opportunities. Your CPA might, if you ask the right questions.
Equity compensation strategy
If you have RSUs, options, or ESPP, the stakes are higher:

items: When to exercise ISOs vs. waiting (AMT implications)
Diversification timing for concentrated positions
ESPP participation optimization
10b5-1 plan structuring

blocks.text: A single equity compensation decision can be worth more than a decade of budget optimization.
Estate planning and protection
As net worth grows, estate planning becomes essential:

items: Revocable living trusts (bypass probate, maintain control)
Irrevocable trusts (asset protection, estate tax reduction)
Beneficiary coordination (often neglected)
Life insurance structuring (ILIT for estate liquidity)

blocks.text: Do you actually understand the trust documents you paid attorneys to create?
Advisor coordination
High-income households often have multiple professionals:

items: CPA for taxes
Estate attorney for legal documents
Financial advisor for investments
Insurance agent for coverage

blocks.text: But who coordinates them? Who ensures the CPA knows about the trust the attorney created? Who verifies decisions actually get implemented?
X1 Wealth: for when budgeting is the easy part
X1 doesn't compete with Monarch or Copilot for expense tracking. We think those apps do budgeting well.
Instead, X1 is the coordination layer above budgeting, where you and your professional team work from one record. On top of that record, it addresses what high earners actually need:
Tax Strategy Discovery: Finds S-corp optimization, entity structuring, and deductions your CPA isn't proactively recommending.
Estate Plan Analysis: Upload your trust documents and get plain-English explanations of what you paid attorneys to create.
Equity Compensation Insights: Helps you understand the tax implications of RSU vesting, option exercises, and ESPP participation.
Advisor Coordination: Single source of truth for your CPA, attorney, and financial advisor, with decision tracking and outcome measurement.
Best for: High-income professionals and business owners who’ve solved the budgeting problem and want to optimize everything else.

What is family office software?

Family office software is a broad category. Some products consolidate investment reporting. Others keep the books or manage trading. X1 prepares cited household reviews, routes each question to the right professional, and saves the answer with its supporting files.
Who is X1 family office software for?

X1 works best when one financial decision touches several entities, documents, or professionals. That may be a household with a trust, business, rental property, private investments, or advisors at several firms. Advisors can also use X1 to prepare a household review.
Is X1 portfolio reporting or family office accounting software?

X1 is built for household reviews, professional handoffs, approvals, and follow-up. If your main need is a general ledger, trading, custody, or institutional portfolio reporting, use a platform built for that job. Our 14-platform comparison explains the differences.
How much does X1 cost?
X1 Wealth costs $97 per month or $997 per year. You can create a free account before choosing a paid membership.
Does X1 replace an advisor, CPA, or attorney?

Your advisor, CPA, and attorney still make the calls that belong to them. X1 helps you bring each person a clear question with the right documents and context. Trading, money movement, tax filing, and legal work stay with the firms you choose.

ctas.text: How the Cash Flow Index works

blocks.text: See which payoff order frees the most monthly cash.
Compare balances and monthly payments to see how much cash a full payoff could release. Use that comparison alongside rates, reserves, and your household priorities.

items: Plug In What You Owe
Mortgage, car, credit cards, business loans, whatever you've got. Balance and monthly payment. Takes 2 minutes.
Compare the Monthly Impact
Each debt gets a Cash Flow Index score. Lower = more cash freed per dollar paid off. The results might surprise you.
Make a Smarter Payoff Plan

blocks.text: Compare the cash each payoff would release.
The Cash Flow Index divides a debt’s balance by its monthly payment. A lower score means a full payoff releases more monthly cash per dollar used.
Balance ÷ monthly payment
For a $5,000 balance with a $250 monthly payment, the score is 20. Paying that balance in full would release $250 per month.
Use this alongside interest rates, available reserves, and loan terms. The score compares cash flow efficiency; it does not decide the right payoff order for your household.
